Plight of HSCL 
* 142. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRA PILLAI: Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state; 
(a) whether the Prime Minister had received a memorandum signed by 57 
Members of Parliament about the plight of Hindustan Steelworks Construction 
Limited (HSCL); 
(b) if so, what are the salient points by the MPs therein; and 
(c) what steps Government have taken on each point raised in the 
memorandum? 
6 

[6 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI DILIP 
RAY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A Memorandum dated nil signed by 57 MPs was received and  
acknowledged on 16th July, 1998 by me Hon'ble Prime Minister. The main  
points raised are as below: 
Major jobs in steel plants are being off loaded to private builders  despite 
HSCL's main activities connected to steel plants from early stages .The price 
preference of 10% allowed by Government has not been adhered to. In some 
cases, HSCL has been L-I, but the jobs have been given to private builders. In 
addition, HSCL's claims have also been withheld/disputed. Thus there is 
shortage of working capital with HSCL. 
The request is to advise/intruct the concerned Ministries to settle the issues 
listed above. 
(c) HSCL was established in 1964 primarily to undertake construction of  
Modern Integrated Steel Plants. It remained a subsidiary of Steel Authority of  
India Limited (SAIL) between>9J3 and 1978. It again became an independent  
company in 1978. The Company had undertaken almost all Civil, Mechanical,  
Structural Erection Works in the Bokaro Steel Plant of SAIL. Similar works  
were undertaken by HSCL during the 4 MT modernisation of Bhilai Steel  
Plant. In addition various job orders like Raw Material H andling Complex,  
Blast Furnace and New Sintering Plant were awarded to HSCL in the  
modernisation of Durgapur Steel Plant. HSCL has been in the process of  
obtaining job orders, and of late, has diversified its activities in the non -steel 
sector like housing, power, roads and bridges and oil. Through HSCL remaiend 
L-I in a number of bids and inspite of the purchase preference of 10% permitted 
by me Government, it has not been able to get the requisite assistance from  
various central PSUs/Central Government Departments. This may have been  
because of its limited experience in some of the fields and also due to its  
accumulated losses incurred over the years and reflected in the balance sheet.  
HSCL has been getting its claims settled with various agencies. Also, SAIL and 
HSCL have resolved to settle their outstanding claims and dues through a  
process of mutual conciliation. 
Ministry of Steel has taken up with Central Government Ministries/Agencies 
in addition to various State Government' Departments/ Agencies with requests 
to award me jobs in their projects to HSCL. Government has sanctioned a 
Revival Package for HSCL in July, 1999. It is expected mat with the scuccessful 
7

implementation of the Revival Package, the performance of HSCL will 
improve.

*143. DR. M.N. DAS: Will the Minis ter of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any special attention is being paid for renovation of the capital 
city of Bhubaneswar in Orissa after it was devastated by the recent super cyclone; 
and

and (b). The Government of India has sanctioned the following amounts to

The total assistance sanctioned by Housing and Urban Development 
Corporation (HUDCO) for Orissa (including Bhubaneswar) under housing is

Imposition of Labour Laws by Developed Countries 
†* 145. SHRI JANESHWAR MISRA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that America and other developed countries are trying 
to impose labour tews through World Trade Organisation inspite of the failure 
of Seattle talks; 
(b) if so, what strategy Government have formulated to frustrate such efforts 
of the developed countries; and  
(c) whether Government are trying to make domestic labour laws effective 
and in the interest of the labourers? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) Attempts were made by many developed countries, to introduce 
the linkage between trade and core labour standards in the future work 
programme of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) at the Seattle Ministerial 
Conference. However, India and other developing countries effectively opposed 
such an inclusion. No formal proposals have been made post -Seattle in WTO 
is this regard by any of the developed countries, but pressure i n future for 
inclusion of this issue in the work programme of WTO cannot be ruled out. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi:  
10 

[6 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) India has been trying to garner support of other developing and like 
minded group of countries for preventing inclusion of this linkage betwee n 
Trade and Labour Standards in the future work programme of the WTO. India 
has also been taking the stand that International Labour Organisation (ILO) is 
the right forum for discussion on issues relating to Labour Standards. 
(c) International Labour Standards , espescially the ILO Core Conventions 
have greatly influenced the enactment of labour laws in India. Labour Laws 
are enforced through inspections by the Central and State Government 
machinery. The Government will continue their efforts for effective 
implementation of Labour laws to protect the interest of the labour. 
Computation of Rate of Industrial Production 
†*146  SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
DR. D. MASTHAN: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to stale: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to include the 
production of 543 items to determine the rate of index of industrial production; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that so far 342 items were included to determine 
the rate of the index of industrial production; and 
(d) if so, what is the reason for including these new items and the names of 
these items? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) to (d) The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is a monthly 
index compiled and released by Central St atistical Organisation (CSO) to 
measure changes in the volume of production in physical terms. In order to 
accurately reflect the growth rate in the industrial sector, the base period of 
the index has been changed from time to time to reflect the changing structure 
of the industrial economy. The latest revision has made the base year 1993 -94 
from the earlier base year 1980 -81. The revised indices were released on 27th 
May, 1998. 
The revision of the coverage of items and industries as. well as the technique 
of construction has changed. Consequently, 543 items have been included 
compared to 352 items in the earlier IIP (Base 1980-81).

Automatic route for FDI 
*149. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2000] 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to allow foreign 
direct investment on automatic route in most of the key industrial sectors; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether the FDI cap in different sectors has also been hiked; and 
(d) what steps have been taken to protect the Indian industry from predatory 
take over by multinational giants? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Government, in its commitment towards 
economic reforms, have announced the new Foreign Direct Investment (F DI) 
Policy thereby placing all items/ activities under the automatic route for Foreign 
Direct Investment (FDI), Non-Resident Indians (NRI) and Overseas Corporate 
Body (OCB) investment except the following: 
1. All proposals that require and industrial Licence which include (i) the 
item requiring and Industrial Licence under the Industries 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1951; (ii) foreign investment 
being more than 24% in the equity capital of units manufacturing 
items reserved for small scale industries; and  (iii) all items which 
require and Industrial Licence in terms of the locational policy 
notified by Government under the New Industrial Policy of 1991. 
2. All proposals in which the foreign collaborator has a previous 
venture/tie-up in India. The modalities p rescribed in Press Note No. 
18 dated 14.12.1998 of 1998 series, shall apply in such cases. 
3. All proposals relating to acquisition of shares in an existing Indian 
company in favour of a foreign/NRI/OCB investor. 
4. AH proposals falling outside notified sectoral  policy/caps or under 
sectors in which FDI is not permitted and/or whenever any investor 
chooses to make an application to the FIPB and not to avail of the 
automatic route. 
All proposals for investment in public sector units as also for EOU/ EPZ/ 
EHTP/STP units would qualify for automatic route subject to above parameters. 
(c) FDI caps in some sectors have been enhanced in consultation and with  
the recommendations of the concerned Administrative Ministries/Departments. 
(d) FDI is not considered a threat to an efficient domestic industry.  
However, while considering FDI proposals, a declaration is obtained from 
20 

[6 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the applicant whether the foreign collaborator has any previous joint venture 
or technology transfer/trademark agreement in the same or allied field in India, 
the detailed circumstances in which it is considered necessary to set up a new 
joint venture/enter into new technology transfer (including trade mark), and 
proof that the new proposal would not in any way jeopardise the interest of the 
existing joint venture or technology/trade mark partner or other stake holders. 
For induction of Foreign/NRI/OCB equity in existing Indian company, a 
copy of the Board Resolution of the existing Indian company is called for. 
For induction of FDI beyond 24% in the activities reserved for small scale 
industry sector, undertaking an export obligation of 50% is mandatory.

Protection to Domestic Automobile Industry 
* 153. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to allow import of 
used cars from 2001; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether any stu dy has been conducted to asses its effect on Indian 
automobile industry; 
(d) if so. the findings thereof; 
(e) what happened to the domestic automobile industry in other developing 
countries where such steps were taken; and 
(f) what steps Government propose to take to safeguard domestic automobile 
22 

[6 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
industry? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) to (f) Cars are classified under Exim Code No. 87.03 of 
ITC(HS) Classifications of Export and Import Items, 1997—2002, and import 
of these items is presently restricted. In view of India's International commitments, 
all quantitative restrictions on imports maintained by India for balance of 
payment reasons are required to be removed by 1.4.2001. 
Research and Information System for the Non Aligned and Other Developing 
Countries (RIS), an autonomous body under the Ministry of External Affairs, 
Government of India, has conducted a study on behalf of Association of Indian 
Automobile Manufacturers on the WTO Regime and its  implications for the 
Indian Automobile Industry. This study has stated that the implementation of 
the commitments undertaken by India as a member of the WTO will have far 
reaching implications for the automobile industry in India. As regards the impact 
on the domestic automobile industry in other developing countries, this study 
has stated that the countries which have allowed the import of second hand 
(used) vehicles have not been successful in establishing a competitive 
automobile industry. 
However, even after removal of quantitative restrictions, the imports will 
still be subject to applicable tariffs, technical standards and environmental and 
safety norms. These measures singly or in combination can be appropriately 
used to create a level playing field for the domestic automobile industry. A 
decision on this issue will be taken in due course after examining all relevant 
aspects.

*157. SHRI PRAFULL GORADIA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:

September, 1999, which had upheld that India's Quantitative Restrictions (QRs)

implementation, as mutually agreed between USA and India will finally 
expire on 1st April, 2001 by which date the existing QRs on all 1429 tariff 
lines at the eight digit level will have to be removed by India.

item has yet been shifted to the Special Import Licence list.

impact of tobacco is as below.: 
Recognizing the indisputable scientific evi dence establishing that tobacco 
consumption in any form and exposure to environmental tobacco smoke are 
casually linked to numerous causes of death, disease and disability, 
Recognizing also that cigarettes are among the most highly engineered 
consumer products, designed to create and maintain addiction and containing 
over 4000 compounds, many of which are pharmacologically active, toxic, 
mutagenic and carcinogenic, 
Recognizing further that 4 million people die each year from tobacco related 
diseases and that this number is expected to rise to 10 million deaths per year 
within the next 25 years, with 70% of these deaths occurring in developing 
countries, 
Deeply concerned about the global spread of the tobacco epidemic and the 
dramatic increase in the worldwid e consumption and production of cigarettes 
and other tobacco products in the last several decades, particularly in 
developing countries, 
Deeply concerned also about the escalation in smoking and other forms of 
tobacco consumption especially by women, child ren and indigenous peoples 
worldwide, 
Deploring all direct and indirect advertizing, marketing, promotion, 
sponsorship and other practices by the tobacco industry aimed at encouraging 
the use of tobacco by children and young adults, 
28 

[6 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Recognizing that the tobacco epidemic is a problem of global dimension 
that calls for immediate national action and the widest possible cooperation by 
all countries in an effective and coordinated international response, 
Recognizing also that The World Bank report has clearly shown that tobacco 
price increase, tobacco advertising bans and controls on smoking in public 
places are effective strategies for reducing tobacco consumption, 
Mindful of the difficulties in adopting and implementing effective  national 
tobacco control programmes, including comprehensive tobacco control 
legislation in countries in which public health resources are limited and 
tobacco industry pressure is overwhelming, 
Recalling Article 1 of the Constitution of the World Health O rganisation 
which provides that "that enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health 
is one of the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction as to 
race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition," 
Recognizing the ne ed for international consensus on the right to be fully 
informed about the addictive and damaging nature of nicotine and the right to 
a somke-free environment, 
Emphasizing the contribution that non -governmental organizations, 
including health professional bodies, women, youth, consumer, and 
environmental groups, academic institutions, media, private industry, hospitals 
and other members of civil society make to tobacco control efforts, 
Therefore, we the participants at the WHO International Conference on 
Global Tobacco Control Law: Towards a WHO Framework Convention on 
Tobacco Control, strongly recommend that: 
1. Governments urgently develop and implement multisectoral national 
tobacco control strategies, including comprehensive tobacco control 
legislation. To this end, governments should establish mechanisms to 
monitor and enforce implementation of all tobacco control laws and 
regulations. 
2. Governments support the development, ratification and 
implementation of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco 
Control (FCTC) to encourage comprehensive national tobacco control 
action and global coordination on aspects of tobacco control that 
transcend national boundaries. The WHO FCTC and key related 
protocols should be adopted by 2003 or earlier. 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2000] 
3. The complex circumstances faced by developing countries in 
implementing effective national tobacco control strategies should be 
addressed in FCTC. The FCTC should include a mechanism to assist 
countries in which public health resources are limited and tobacco 
industry pressure is overwhelming in developing and implementing 
comprehensive national tobacco control programmes. Industrialized 
countries should support the establishment and strengthening of 
effective national tobacco control programmes in developing 
countries. Such programmes should include, but not be limited to, 
building sustainable capacity in national and international tobacco 
control strategies, including legislation, assisting with the treatment 
of tobacco dependence and assisting res earch into alternative 
livelihoods for tobacco workers and alternative uses of tobacco. 
4. The tobacco industry be held publicly accountable at the national and 
international level through legislation, litigation and other means. 
5. Given the impact of tobacco p roducts on public health, the WHO 
should coordinate closely with regional and international trade 
organizations to ensure that tobacco control measures and trade 
liberalization measures are complementary. 
6. Non-governmental organizations, including health pr ofesssional 
bodies, women, youth, consumer and environmental groups, academic 
institutions, private industry, media, hospitals and other members of 
civil society, should take an active role in tobacco control initiatives 
at the sub-national, national, regional and global levels. 
(c) The Committee on Subordinate Legislation (Tenth Lok Sabha) in its 
22nd Report had made several recommendation's primarily intended to 
discourage the use of tobacco and tobacco products. The Government is 
examining these recommen dations and the draft legislation is under 
consideration of the Government.

1054. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND  
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has sought reforms in the WTO regime; 
(b) if so, what are the details indicating the precise object sought to be 
achieved thereby; 
(c) the moves made and the steps taken to secure such reforms; and 
(d) what trade preferences enjoyed by developing countries under the CATT 
are being denied or diluted under the WTO regime? 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [6 March, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) and (b) India has been seeking  reforms in the WTO regime by 
way of redressal of the existing asymmetries and inequities in several of the 
WTO Agreements, and the non-realization of expected benefits from Agreements 
such as textiles and agriculture by the developing countries in general  and 
India in particular. India has also effectively articulated the manner in which 
the special and differential treatment provisions of the WTO Agreements have 
remained virtually inoperative and how, even in areas where developing 
countries acquire,competitiveness, antidumping or anti -subsidies investigations 
are initiated in increasing numbers by the developed countries to leny them 
market access. India has also resolutely opposed moves to introduce linkages 
between labour and trade or any further widening of the environmental window 
under WTO agreements, as this may result in disguised protectionism affecting 
the market access of developing countries. The major objective to be achieved 
through these efforts is to bring the development dimension to the forefront, in 
order that the multilateral trading system subserves the stated objective of the 
WTO Agreements of raising standards of living, ensuring full employment 
and a large and steadily growing volume of real income and Effective demand, 
and expanding the production of trade in goods and services..." 
(c) India has been following a two rpronged strategy! in this regard. On the  
one hand, a national consensus on various issues as were raised in the preparatory 
process of the Third WTO Ministerial Conference, has been evolved in  
consultations with the major stakeholders, including industry, national level  
political parties and trade unions, research institutions, trade experts and"civil  
society. On the other hand diplomatic initiatives were taken to garner support  
from like-minded countries, such as the SAARC, the G-15 Group comprising of 
seventeen countries and the G-77 Group of developing countries. 
(d) During the earlier rounds of GATT, till the Kennedy Round, the  
developing countries were not expected to t ake on many of the obligations  
which developed on many of the developed countries. However, under the  
Uruguay Round which gave birth to the WTO, developing countries have  
taken on substantial obligations on trade in goods, services and Intellecutal 
Property Rights. The Special and Differential treatment provisions other than  
the provisions providing for a longer transition period or higher dimensions in 
favour of developing countries, as contained in most of the WTO Agreements,  
are only in the nature, of the "best endeavour' provisions and have not been

1066.   SHRI S.RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: 
SHRI E. BALANANDAN: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have lifted Quantitative Restriction (QR) on imports 
of 1400 American products into the country; 
(b) if so, what prompted Government to take such a decision just after the 
Winter Session was adjourned on 23rd December, 1999; 
(c) whether Government are aware that this lifting of QR would endanger 
India's economic security; and 
(d) if so, as to why India has kept it secret and US has exposed it? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) No, Sir. There is no lifting of Quantitative Restriction (QR) on 
1400 American Products. However, consequent to the ruling and 
recommendations of the Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) of the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO) that India was no longer justified in maintaining 
quantitative restrictions (QRs) on import on balance of payments (BoP) 
grounds in a dispute filed by the United States o f America, India and the USA 
have signed a bilateral agreement which has determined the reasonable 
44 

[6 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
period of time (RPT) for implementing the above rulings and recommendations. 
Accordingly, existing QRs on U,29 tariff lines  3a eight digit level maintained 
on balance of payments grounds are to be removed by 1st April, 2001. 
(b) Following adoption of the Appellate Body and Panel Reports by the 
DSB on 22nd September, 1999 a easonable period of time had to be 
determined for India to  implement the rulings and recommendations of the 
DSB. The RPT can be determined either through arbitration or through bilateral 
agreement between parties to the dispute. The bilateral agreement has to be 
reached within 45 days of date of adoption, unless both sides agree to an 
extension of time period India and the USA held bilateral discussions during 
the said period of 45 days but could not arrive at an understanding. 
Consequently, both sides moved the WTO for extension of this time period a 
number of times, which was granted. Finally, after prolonged discussions India 
and the USA reached an agreement on this issue, which was jointly notified, to 
the WTO on 28th December, 1999. 
(c) Since, QRs on these items are still to be lifted, exact impact of removal of 
QRs on India's economic security cannot be quantified. However, the removal 
of QRs on 1285 items which has been effected since 1997, did not have any 
serious implications. 
(d) No, Sir, as has been explained in answer to (b) above.

(i)   New Growth Centre Scheme: With a view to promoting 
industrialisation of backward areas in the country, the Government 
had announced the Growth Centre Scheme in June, 1988 under which 
71 growth centres were proposed to be set up in various States. Each 
growth centre is to be developed at  an estimated project cost of Rs.

(ii)    Transport Subsidy Scheme: This scheme was introduced in July, 1971

the scheme, subsidy ranging from 50% to 90% is admissible on 
transport cost incurred on movement of raw materials and finished 
goods from the designated rail heads/ports upto the location of the 
industrial units and vice versa. The scheme is valid upto 31st March, 
2000. However, the scheme has been extended upto 31st March, 2007 
in respect of the North Eastern Region. 
(iii)    Capital Investment Subsidy Scheme: This scheme w as notified in 
June, 1998 under the Prime Minister's new initiatives for the North 
Eastern Region. Under the scheme, subsidy at the rate of 15% of the 
investment in plant and machinery, subject to a ceiling of Rs. 30 lakh 
is payable to industries located i n the growth centres. The subsidy 
amount is to be disbursed through the North Eastern Development 
Finance Corporation Limited. 
(iv)    Central Interest Subsidy Scheme: This scheme has been formulated 
for the North Eastern Region in the year 1999. Under the  scheme, 
interest subsidy at the rate of 3% on the working capital loan is payable 
for a period of ten years to the new units set up in the North Eastern 
Region, after the units go into production.

the industrial units in the North Eastern Region, in July, 1999. The scheme 
is effective for a period often years. Under the scheme, all industrial units set

reimbursement of the insurance premium paid by the units.

The informal system of workers' participation in decision making operates 
through Quality Circles, Suggestion schemes, Shop -Improvement Groups and 
by direct contribution of employees to production and productivity at the 
shop-floor. 
The national Level Bipartite form in the Steel Industry, viz., National Joint 
Committee for Steel Industry (NJCS) has emerged as a unique forum, which 
comprises of management and workers' representatives both from public and 
private sector (TISCO) including Central and Plant level and the All -India 
Unions Representatives from the Steel Industry, such as, INTUC, AITUC, HMS, 
CITU and other recognised trad e union organisations of the steel plants. The 
cooperation, mutual trust and joint decision making in NJCS has percolated 
down to the Shop Floor level Committees and has helped in reinforcing healthy 
industrial relations climate and bipartite culture. This  has led to enhanced 
production and productivity in the steel Industry.

*163.  SHRI NILOTPAL BASU:‡ 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: 
Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the TRAI has referred to cellular telecom 
services as a premium service and not a utility service in its documents; 
(b) if so, the response of Government in accepting this assessment; and 
(c) if such a service is indeed a premium service, the reasons for foregoing 
the deemed payment from private cellular telecoms and going ahead with 
migration, package and claiming this as 'public good"?

PASWAN): (a) to (c) A statment is laid on the Table of the House.

Statement 
(a) and (b) While the cellular service has been referred by TRAI in some 
of their documents as a premium service, it is at the same time generally 
perceived to be of considerable utility to the users to this service. 
(c) While approving New Telecom Policy — 1999 (NTP -99), the 
government considered, inter alia, that it is in public interest for the New 
Telecom Policy to be uniformaly applicable throughout the country. 
Therefore, the policy regarding migration of the existing licensees of Basic 
and Cellular Services to the NTP -99 regime of revenue sharing arrangement 
was formulated and approved. This would ensure growth of telecom sector by 
bringing in multipoly, better accessability and improved/ cost effective 
service to cu stomers and is important for achieving the objectives of New 
Telecom Policy.

be of considerable utility to the users of this service. I think the statement is

Communications saying that there was a specific need for studying the

to know whether such a study was made. I would also like to know whether 
such study reflected this basic fact that cellular service is not a utility service 
but a premium service.

Settlement of River Water Disputes 
†*164.   DR. D. MASTHAN: 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Commission for Integrated Water Resources 
Development has expressed its opinion that the existing law is inadequate to 
settle the river water disputes; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; 
(c) whether it is a fact that several d isputes regarding sharing of river 
waters are pending; if so, what are these disputes together with the names of 
the States where these disputes exist; and 
(d) the steps Government propose to take to settje these disputes? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (DR. C.P. THAKUR): (a) to 
(d) In order to ensure that awards of inter -state water tribunals are given 
within a reasonable period of time as also the effectiveness of such awards, 
National Commission for Integrated Water Resources Development Plan has 
recommended to amend the Inter State Water Disputes Act, 1956. An 
Implementation Cell in the National Water Development Agency has been 
constituted to examine recommendations' of the National Commission and 
suggest to Union Government about the implementability or o ther-wise of the 
recommendations and to suggest modalities for impementation of such 
recommendations, as found implementable. An Advisory Committee under 
the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Water Commission has been 
constituted for assisting the implemen tation cell in examining the 
recommendations. 
The Inter -State Water Disputes viz. Ravi -Beas Water Dispute between 
Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan and the Cauvery Water Disputes between 
Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and the Union Territory of Pondicherry were  
referred to the Tribunals under the provisions of the Inter State Water Dispute 
Act, 1956 (ISWD Act, 1956) for adjudication in April, 1986 and June, 1990 
respectively. Ravi-Beas Waters Tribunal has submitted its fact finding report 
on 30.1.1987. Party Sta tes and the Central Government have sought 
explanation/guidance under Section 5(3) of ISWD Act, 1956. The Cauvery 
Water Disputes Tribunal has passed an interim order on June 25, 1991.

Although there may be some apprehensions regarding the impact of 
economic reforms on the different sectors of the economy, these do not 
appear to be well -founded on factual evidence. The economic reforms 
initiated in the last few years have had a favourable impact in terms of 
acceleration in overall growth of the economy, build up of a comfortable

†*180. SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL:

41

RAJYA SABHA                     [7 March, 2000] 
(b) whether Government have assessed the capacity regarding storage of 
rain water; 
(c) if so, what is the capacity; and 
(d) the schemes formulated by Government to utilise the capacity? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (DR. C.R THAKUR): (a) to 
(d) India receives a rainfall of about 4000 billion cu.m. every year. Out of this 
about 1869 billion cu. m. appears as runoff in the various rivers of the 
country. The replenishable Ground Water is around 432 billion cu.m. The 
requirement of the country, upto 2025 AD can be met through optimal 
utilisation of these renewable water resources. 
The utilisable runoff by conventional methods has been assessed as 690 
Billion Cubic Metre (BCM). A live storage capacity of 176.73 BCM has been 
created by construction of large dams & medium projects upto 1995 
including about 3 BCM capacity created by medium & small dams. Projects 
to add an additional capacity of about 75.42 BCM a re under construction and 
132.32 BCM are under planning. 
Government of India is also promoting Rain Water Harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, Artificial Recharge of Ground Water 
and roof -top rain water harvesting under the Sector Reform Proj ect of 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural 
Development for which technical and financial assistance is provided to the 
State Government and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water 
Board has also taken up pilot stu dies for artificial ground water recharge. The 
rooftop rain water harvestiang structures are quite large in number and are 
mostly at individual level and, therefore it is difficult to assess their storage 
capacity. Its contribution towards storage can only  be marginal in comparison 
to the storage through conventional methods.

Holding of Hijacked Plane at Amritsar Airport 
1223.SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN:  
        SHRI AMAR SINGH:  
        SHRIMATI JAYAPRADA NAHATA: 
SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state:— 
(a) the minute to minute details of circumstances leading to the taking off 
the hijacked Indian Airlines plane IC 814 from Amritsar. 
(b) the factors responsible for delay in timely action in preventing the 
plane's take off; and 
(c) whether responsibility for causing delay has bee n fixed; if so, the 
details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) 
Upon refusal of permission to land at Lahore, the hijacked aircraft IC -814 
landed at Rajasansi Airport, Amritsar at 1900 hrs. on 24.12.99. The hijackers 
demanded immediate refuelling. The plane was slowly moving around on the 
runway and refused to come to the parking bay. The Aerodrome Committee 
tried a couple of times to engage the hijackers in a dialogue. But the hijackers 
flatly refused to come on the Radi o Telephone (RT). At 1949 hrs., on citing 
the bowser close to the aircraft, it took off without ATC clearance. When the 
aircraft landed at Amritsar, concrete and specific information in respect of the 
numbers, nationality, weaponry, professionalism and com mitment of the 
hijackers was scantly and speculative. On the other hand, messages being 
received from the hijacked aircraft were tense and demanding. Precipitate 
action, in the absence of even basic information was judged as being fraught 
with unacceptable levels of risk. 
(b) and (c) On the occurence of the hijacking, institutional mechanisms to 
deal with situation were immediately put into action. The Crisis Management 
Group (CMG) and the Central Committee met to address the evolving 
situation. The NSG Tas k Force was also placed on full alert. On the basis of 
available facts, the CMG came to conclusion that the aircraft could not go 
anywhere unless refuelled. The CMG and others concerned acted in the best 
possible way under the given situation.

100 

[7 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
State Finances, A Study of budgets of 1999- 2000, the debt—GDP ratio of the 
State governments is projected to increase to 20.5% at the end —March, 2000 
as compared to 19.4% in 1998-99. At page S-44 of this Report the outstanding 
liability of the States is estimated to be Rs. 409,258 crores by March, 2000 
which is 19.9% higher than Rs. 341,259 crore at March end 1999.

reference of the Eleventh Finance Commission which is currently in office.

1317. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the existing system of superintendence and control of Supreme Court 
and High Courts on the functioning of the lower curts; 
(b) whether the system has worked successfully, if so,, the number of 
judicial o fficers punished for malfesance and misjudgement during the last 
three years; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) Under the 
Constitution of India, there is a single integrated system of Courts for the 
Union as well as the States which administer both Union and State laws, and 
at the head of the entire system stands the Supreme Court of India. Below the 
Supreme Court of India stand the High Courts of the different States and under 
each High Court there is a hierarchy of other courts called subordinate courts.  
According to article 227 of the Constitution of India, every High Court 
shall have superintendence over all court s and tribunals throughout the 
territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction. The said article further 
provides that the High Court may call for returns from such courts; make and 
issue general rules and prescribe forms for regulating the practice and 
proceedings of such courts; and prescribe forms in which books, entries and 
accounts shall be kept by the officers of any such courts.

and courts subordinate thereto including the posting and promotion of, and the 
grant of leave to, persons belonging to the judicial service of a State and 
holding any post inferior to the post of district judge, in the High Court.

Cleaning of the Ganga 
1349. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Mi nister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state. 
(a) whether a major project for cleaning the Ganga was launched during 
the Prime Ministership of late Shri Rajiv Gandhi; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the results achieved so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE  MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BUOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. Ganga Action Plan, Phase -I was launched during the Prime Ministership 
of Shri Rajeev Gandhi in June, 1985. 261 schemes of pollution abatement of 
various categories such as int erception, diversion and treatment of municipal 
wastewater, installation of crematoria, river front development works and low 
cost sanitation etc. were sanctioned at a cost of Rs. 462.04 crore in 25 class -
"I" towns in the three States of Uttar Pradesh, Bih ar and West Bengal. 258 
schemes have since been completed which include 32 sewage treatment 
plants. The total expenditure incurred so far is Rs. 451.70 crore under this 
programme. With this, out of the 873 million litres per day of domestic waste 
water targeted 
1 67 

RAJYA SABHA                    [7 March, 2000] 
for interception, diversion and treatment, a capacity to treat 835 million litres 
per day of wastewater has been created. With the completion of these 
schemes, it has been possible to minimise the organic pollution reaching the 
river Ganga. Water quality of river has shown improvement wherever 
completed works are functional. However, there has been only an incidental 
reduction in the level of microbial pollution of the treated sewage reaching the 
river. 
Ganga Action Plan, Phase —"II" has been approved in stages by the 
Government of India between April, 1993 to October, 1996.About 1861 
million litres per day of domestic wastewater is targeted for interception, 
diversion and treatment under this phase.  The total sanctioned cost is Rs. 
1276.26 crore and this includes the following schemes for implementation in 
95 towns in 5 States. 
1. Interception and diversion 
2. Sewage treatment plant 
3. Electric and wood-based crematoria 
4. Low cost sanitation 
5. River front development works. 
Mingling for North-South rivers 
†1350. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
 SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided for considering the possibilities to 
mingle the rivers flowing in the North and South India; 
(b) if so, the action taken by Government in this regard; and 
(c) the names of the rivers of the country identified for mingling? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) The 
erstwhile Ministry of Irrigation (now Ministry of Water Resources) and 
Central Water Commission had in 1980 formulated a National Perspective 
Plan for Water Resources Development which envisages inter linkages 
between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water 
from surplus basins to water deficit basins for optimum utilisation of water 
resources. The Peninsular rivers are Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, 
Cauvery, Vaigai,

[7 March, 2000]                      RAJYA SABHA 
Parbati, Kalisindh, Chambal, Damanganga, Pinjal, Par, Tapi, Narmada, Ken, 
Betwa, Pamba, Achankovil, Bedti, Varda, Netravati and Hemavati. The 
Himalayan Rivers are Kosi, Mechi, Ghagra, Gandak, Ganga,  Yamuna, Sarda, 
Sabarmati, Sone, Brahmaputra, Domadar and Subernarekha. The Government

1355. DR. M.N. DAS: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be

Environment & Forests has not yet been obtained by the Government of Bihar.

Generation of Irrigation Capacity 
† 1358. DR. D.MASTHAN: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have made an estimate of the 
requirement of irrigation in the country; 
(b) if so, to what extent irrigation capacity is required to be generated; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that a time bound plan has been prepared to 
meet this requirement; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Net 
Sown Area in the country is 142.82 million hectares as per Land Use Statistics 
brought out by the Mi nistry of Agriculture for the year 1996 -97 (latest). 
Against this, Ultimate Irrigation Potential (UIP) in the country has been 
assessed as 139.89 million hecatres (m.ha.) Out of this, irrigation capacity of 
89.56 m.ha has already been created by the end of  the Eighth Five Year Plan, 
leaving 50.33 m.ha. of irrigajion capacity to be generated. 
(c) and (d) Creation of irrigation capacity is a continuous process and for 
this purpose the State Governments take up major, medium, and minor 
irrigation projects. In the Ninth Five Year Plan, target of creating additional 
irrigation capacity of 17.05 m.ha. comprising 9.81 m.ha. from major and 
medium irrigation projects and 7.24 m.ha. from minor irrigation schemes, has 
been set. Outlays of Rs. 42644 crore for major and medium irrigation sector 
and Rs. 8985 crore for minor irrigation sector have been provided in the Ninth 
Plan (State Sector) for development of irrigation facilities in the country. 
Besides plan allocation, the Union Government is also providing Central Loa n 
Assistance to the States through Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme 
for expeditious completion of on -going major & medium irrigation projects, 
which are languishing for want of funds. Also the Government of India has 
prepared a National Perspectiv e Plan for transfer of water from surplus areas 
to water deficit areas. As per preliminary assessment, it is envisaged that 
additional irrigation capacity of 35 million hectares would be feasible through 
inter-basin transfer of water.

*181. SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA:† 
SARDAR GURCHARAN SINGH TOHRA: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any proposal under active consideration of 
Government to construct a new capital for the State of Haryana and award 
whole of Chandigarh to Punjab on permanent basis; and

of transfer of Chandigarh to Punjab is linked with the resolution of other issues 
arising out of the territorial claims put forward by Punjab and Haryana 
consequent upon the enactment of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966. The 
Central Government would like the concerned State Governments to sort out 
their differences amicably through discussion and mutual accommodation.

Statement-II 
Resolutions of the Chief Ministers'/Power Ministers' Conference held 
on 26.02.2000 
The Power Ministers' Conference took note of the impending difficult 
situation facing the power supply industry in the country due to continuing 
decline in commercial viability of the sector as a whole. 
It noted the fact that:—  
1. Outstanding dues of CPSUs have been increasing and have now 
reached Rs. 23,000 crores. This trend if maintained, would adversely 
affect their current operations apart from inhibiting their future 
expansion plans. 
2. Financial closure for private power projects is becoming increasingly 
difficult. 
3. The States are unable to finance new projects on their own. 
4. Increases in budgetary support from State Governments as well as 
Central Government for this sector is not feasible due to fiscal 
deficits. 
II. The primary factors responsible for this unsustainable  
financial situation are: 
(i) Theft and pilferage at the macro level are estimated to be over Rs. 
20,000 crores per annum. 
(ii) Technical losses in transmission and distribution for the country are 
also too high. 
(iii) Large number of the thermal stations in the state sector run at an 
operational efficiency of less than 40%. 
(iv) The average annual operational losses of the State Power Sector for 
the country is over Rs. 12,000 crores. 
III. It was also  recognised that the cross subsidies cannot be  
sustained if industrial tariffs make Industry non -competitive in the  
new environment of increasing globalisation with elimination of  
quantitative and other restrictions. It becomes necessary to ensure  
that Indian Industry is not handicapped by unsatisfactory power 
10 

[8 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
supply or by tariff which makes it non -competitive. Further, the consumer, 
including the farmer has a legitimate claim for uninterrupted good quality 
power supply. His willingness to pay reasonable costs is underestimated. 
Resolutions 
1. The Power Ministers' resolved after taking into account all the  
problems facing the power sector, that with the intention of achieving  
commercial viability and providing power at reasona ble rate to all,  
reform must be undertaken with determination, vigor and a sense of  
urgency. Delay in reform only increases the financial cost of reforms,  
and the burden of liabilities only increases. Reforms must begin to  
show results within the next 2 -3 years. The key elements of the  
reform strategy are:—  
a. Energy Audit at all levels. 
b. Time-bound programme of 100% metering of all consumers 
by December 2001. 
c. Reduction and finally, elimination of power theft within a 
specified time frame. 
d. Strengthening/upgradation of sub-transmission and distribution 
system by taking sub-station as an unit on a priority basis. 
2. If the above appears unattainable in the existing set up 
corporatization/cooperatization/privatization of distribution, would have to 
be undertaken. 
3. Since a large number of thermal stations within the State sector are 
running at a PLF below 40%, immediate Renovation and Modernisation 
including Life Extension would need to be undertaken on an urgent basis. 
Similarly, R&M/LE would require to be u ndertaken for old hydel power 
plants on priority. 
4. Effective functioning of State Electricity Regulatory  
Commissions is essential for rationalization of tariff, and balancing  
the interests of the consumer and the need for commercial viability of  
the utilities in the environment where private sector participation in  
the industry is expected to gradually increase. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2000] 
5. Unboundling and corporatization of State Electricity Boards/ bench -
marking through separate distribution profit c entres/ corporations/companies 
may facilitate the Regulatory Commissions in promoting competition within the 
power supply industry-competition being the key to lower prices. 
6. It was noted that the power system network in country has an 
unmatched reach to co nsumers and with the installation of optic fibre cables 
along the existing power lines using its right of way, it has the potential of 
generating very large resources in the coming years by providing facilities for 
multipurpose communication including cabl e TV, IT services, Telecom 
services, etc. Hence efforts need to be made to creatively tap this potential 
source of large revenue from convergence. 
7. In order to promote reforms, a new draft central legislation which 
obviates the need for separate enactments for the States, is being considered. 
The draft Bill submitted by the NCAER would form the basis for a national 
debate and a consensus on the contents of the new Bill. The States would be 
sending their detailed comments on this draft Bill, to the Ministry o f Power 
at the earliest.

1451. SHRI RAMACHAN DRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of MINES

MINERALS DR. (SHRIMATI): RITA VERMA: The entire issue of revision 
of coal royalty rates was examined recently in the Department of Coal and a 
decision taken not to increase the coal royalty rates on following grounds:—

depression. Any increse in coal royalty rates will deepen this crisis.

Limited (CIL) subsidiaries name ly, Eastern Coalfields limited (ECL)

Statement II 
Present Status of Reforms m States 
The objective of power sector reforms is to bring in commercial viability in 
the power supply industry so as to ensure power supply on demand to all 
consumers at reasonable prices. 
In order to achieve this objective, full energy audit, corporatisa- tion and 
unbundling of SEB's may be necessa ry. To the extent effective control on 
power theft does not appear feasible in the public sector, privatisation of 
distribution may have to be undertaken. Effective functioning of State 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions is also an essential component of reforms 
with a view to balanacing the interests of the consumer and the need for 
commercial viability of the utilities. 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2000] 
The status of reforms and restructuring is as under :— 1 SFRC 
Fourteen States (Orissa, Haryana, Andhra P radesh, Uttar Pradesh, 
Karnataka, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Delhi, Gujarat, Madhya Pradsh, 
Arunachal Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan) have either constituted or 
notified the constitution of SFRC. 
A Bill to amend the Electricity Regulatory Commiss ion Act, 1998 has 
been introduced in Lok Sabha on 23.12.1999 to enable two or more States/UTs 
to form a joint Electricity Regulatory Commission. 
2. CORPORATTSATION OF SEBs : 
The SEB's of Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh 
have been unbundled/corporatised. 
3. DISTRIBUTION REFORMS 
Orissa has privatised distribution through four joint venture distribution 
companies where 51% share holding and management control have been handed 
over to private firms. 
The Government of UP plans to privatise distribution in Kanpur and has 
invited price bids for 74% of the share holding of the distribution company 
created for Kanpur. 
The Government of Delhi has commissioned studies to look into the aspect 
of corporatisation and undertaking distribution through joint venture companies. 
Many States are taking action for creating distribution profit centres.

1476. DR. P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) .whether it is a fact that a serious and unprecedented power  
breakdown overtook the whole of Northern India during the first  
week of January, 2000; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether any formal enquiry was instituted into such unseasonal 
breakdown; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) what specific steps have been taken/proposed to be taken to prevent 
the recurrence of such devastating power failure? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) A grid disturbance occurred in 
Northern Regional Power Grid on 6th January, 2000 affecting power supply 
in parts of Northern India. 
(b) The overdrawal from the grid by States /Constituents resulting in 
operation of Northern Regional Grid at low system frequency caused the grid 
disturbance. During first week of January, 2000 intense cold wave conditions 
were prevailing resulting in high power demand in Northern Region while the 
availability was not commensurate with the demand due to less thermal 
generation on account of forced outages of machines in Central /State 
sectors, less hydro generation due to poor water inflows. 
(c) to (e) No forma l enquiry was instituted. A meeting was immediately 
taken after the grid disturbance with all heads of Power Utilities /Constituents 
of Northern Region. The following steps were suggested: 
(i) The system frequency be maintained at all time above 49.0 Hz. 
(ii) All the under -frequency relays be restored/revived to their original 
settings as per the recommendation of NREB to provide adequate load 
relief at the designated frequency levels. 
152 

[8 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) All the States/Constituents to re strict their drawal from the grid to the 
drawal schedule given to them on daily basis. 
(iv) Adequate shunt capacitors be installed/added by all the constituents in 
their respective systems to maintain normal voltage profile.

†1483. SHRI JANESHWAR M ISRA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

drinking water has been made for ten crore people in the country;

shape;

the facility of potable water; and 
(d) what has been the percentage of success rate so far in the National 
Potable Water Mission? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) Water supply is a State subject 
and drinking water facilities are provided under the State Sector Minimum 
Needs Programme (MNP). The Central Government supplements the efforts of 
the States by providing assistance und er the Centrally sponsored Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Accelerated Urban Water Supply 
Programme (AUWSP). 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
161 
 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2000] 
As per the information furnished by the State Governments, as on 1st April 
1999, 97.59% of the rural habitations have access to drinking water facilities. In 
terms of population, out of a rural population of 62.87 crore (1991 census), as 
on 1st April 1999, approximately 61.64 crore have been provided with access to 
drinking water facilities and the coverage is lowest in States of Kerala, 
Nagaland and Punjab. As regard urban population, out of a population of 
23.93 crore as estimated for 31* March, 1997, approximately 21.57 crore have 
been provided with access to drinking water facilities till 31" March, 1997 and 
the coverage is lowest in Dadra & Nagar Haveli (UT) and States of Mizoram 
and Assam. 
All the States have been requested to prepare action plans to provide 
drinking water to all rural habitations in the next five years. The objective could be 
achieved, subject to availability of funds. Similarly, 100% urban population is 
targeted to be provided with safe drinking water facilities in the Ninth Plan 
Period, subject to availability of funds. 
In order to ensure sustainability of the systems created under the Rural Water 
Supply Programme, the Government has initiated action to institutionalise 
community participation in the planning and implementation of the Rural Water 
Supply Schemes.

1505. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state:

removal of quantitative restrictions on our textiles export after the abolition 
in 2005 of the Multifibre Textile Agreement;

competitiveness and efficiency of our textile industry to take full  
advantage of the quota free trade order after 2005?

been a few studies to analyse the impact of post -quota regime on our textile 
and c lothing exports. These studies have emphasised the need for 
modernisation and technological upgradation, human resource development, 
strategic alliances and Foreign Direct Investment so that the industry is 
enabled to successfully meet the competitive envi ronment of post -quota

international trade.

2000—2004 announced recently to provide stability and continuity 
and encourage competitiveness in textile exports. 
(3) Non-Quota Entitlement (NQE) System for encouraging non quota 
exports to quota and non- quota countries has been retained to boost 
exports in apparel sector-value added segment of Indian textiles.

in all spheres of society. The significance of the International Women's Day 
lies in our re-affirmation to improve the condition of women, especially those 
at the margin of society, and empower them to take their rightful place in the 
society. Despite existing policies, women are still a socially disadvantaged 
section of our society. Even within the family, they s uffer discrimination.

lliteracy is still high among women, more so among rural women.

They face a significant drawback on account of health and 
malnutrition. They are the silent sufferers of new diseases, like AIDS.

they are demonstrating before Parliament. They say that a kind of jobless growth 
is taking place in our country. T he level of employment is going down and 
rural poverty has increased. The people are astounded with the announcement 
of the Finance Minister that all the public sector undertakings' share will be 
reduced to 26 per cent. The people are shocked at this annou ncement. Sir, the 
Government has taken up the policy of liberalisation...

policy, but if that policy is not followed by the introduction of land reforms...

the Question Hour. During Question Hour, nothing else but questions are taken 
up.

MR. CHAIRMAN: I am not objecting to their demands. I am only saying 
that the Question Hour will not be suspended. Inviolability of the Question 
Hour is the unanimous decision of the House. The hon. Members should not go 
against their own decision.

*208. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL

professionals who are out of job are facing many problems;

software engineers from india? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) and (b) There are approximately 300,000 Indian software professionals in 
Silicon Valley, USA, most of them extremely well-settled. Out of these, about

San Francisco are in touch with the software engineers through concerned 
Associations, to give all possible help and advice.

Most Favoured Nation Status to Pakistan 
*210. SHRI V.N. GADGIL: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government believe that Pakistan should be declared as a 
terrorist state; 
(b) if so, why is Pakistan still accorded a Most Favoured Nation status 
despite no reciprocity; 
(c) why has not the liberal visa regime for Pakistani visitors been 
terminated when its blatant misuse is well known; and 
(d) what efforts have been made to have it declared as a terrorist state? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) to (d) The facts regarding Pakistan's state sponsorship of terrorism in Jammu 
and Kashmir and elsewhere in India have been effectively and appropriately 
brought before several international fora and have also been raised at high -
level bilateral discussions with world leaders. The international community 
now openly recognises Pakistan's state sponsorship of terrorism and the impact 
this has on the security of the country and the region. 
Contrary to its commitment under the WTO, Pakistan has not extended 
MFN treatment to India. While Government continue to meet its international 
trade obligations under its WTO commitments, they also continue to take all 
necessary actions to protect the country's trade interests vis-a-vis Pakistan. 
Government is of the view that the promotion of people-to-people contacts 
between India and Pakistan contributes to its desire of establishing a relationship 
of peace, friendship and cooperation with that country. While pursuing such an 
approach, Government exercises due vigilance including in its visa policy for 
Pakistani nationals so that the security of the country is safeguarded.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the software industry has been one of the 
fastest growing industries in the electronic sector; 
(b) whether the export of software has recorded a growth of forty three 
percent over the Eighth Plan period reaching $1042 million in 1996- 97 and 
$1749 million in 1997-98; 
(c) whether during the same period, the domestic growth rate was about 
fifty-two percent touching Rs. 2600 crores by 1996- 97 and Rs. 3470 crores in 
1997-98; and 
(d) what steps Government have taken to encourage this industry and 
stimulate further growth in view of the phenomenal sustained growth rate in 
this sector? 
THE MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND MINISTER OF 
INFORMATION T ECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN): (a) to 
(c)Yes, Sir. 
(d) A statement is enclosed. 
Statement 
The Government of India has set up the Ministry of Information 
Technology on 15.10.1999 to facilitate all initiatives in the IT sector including 
Internet, e-commerce, IT education and IT based education. 
18 

[9 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
The Government has accepted the first report of the National IT Task 
Force outlining 108 recommendations of the IT Action Plan. These 
recommendations suggest measures and policies covering a wide spectrum. of 
issues relating to telecommunication, finance banking, revenue, commerce, 
electronics, HRD, defence and rural development to enable India to emerge as 
an Information Technology super power within the next ten years. A target of 
software export of US$50 billion by the year 2008 has been set. The Task Force 
has also recommended a goal of ""IT for AH" by 2008 in India. The second and 
third report of the Task Force address the . issues and strategy for development 
of hardware industry, R&D in the area of IT, manpower training and education. 
All Government Departments are required to spend 2 -3% of their 
budget towards implementation of IT. To induce more investment in R&D in 
computers, a weighted deduction of 125% on the sums paid to any 
university, college or institution or a scientific research association for the 
purpose of scientific, social or statistical research has been provided. 
Many States of India have drawn up comprehensive IT plans and have 
come out with IT policies which will help in creating a conducive 
environment for high growth of high-tech industries. 
Government of India has also formed a Rs. 100 crores National Venture 
Capital Fund in association with the Small Industries Development Bank of 
India (SIDBI), Industrial Dev elopment Bank of India (IDBI) for the IT 
industry particularly for small and medium enterprises. 
Penetration of Personnel Computers (PC) in the country at present is 
slightly more than 3 per 1000 persons. The target is to increase the PC 
penetration to 20 per 1000 person by the year 2008. To push the demand of 
PCs in the country, depreciation on computers has been increased to 60%. 
Government has implemented Internet Service providers (ISPs) Policy, 
ISPs are allowed to set up International Gateways and hire  bandwidth on 
foreign satellites. Public and private sectors have been licensed to provide 
internet services in the country. No licence fee is payable for first five years 
and a nominal fee of one rupee is to be paid after five years. The internet 
policy approved by Governments provides inter -connection of networks and 
setting up of international gateway by the internet service provider 
independent of VSNL. The infrastructure for Internet is proposed to be 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2000] 
upgraded as below: 
(a) Department of Telecom Services (DTS) is setting up national internet 
backbone in the country. 
(b) Internet Service Providers are allowed to set up last mile linkages 
freely by fibre optic or by radio communication. 
(c) The Internet access is also allowed through authorized cable TV. 
The tariff for internet access has been recently reduced. DTS have recently 
offered 20% concession on rental for leased lines taken and used for internet 
applications. Students are being given one time concession on internet accounts 
by DTS. Access to internet on local call basis from the nearest internet node has 
been provided throughout the country except in Andaman and Nicobar Island 
and Leh (J and K). The existing departmental Public Gall Operators (PCO) and 
Subscriber Trunk Dailing (STD) booths are proposed to be upgraded to public 
tele-info/cyber centres. These centres will provide multi -utility services such 
as internet, e-mail access and internet libraries. 
To provide the legal framework for transaction on Internet and e-commerce, 
Information Technology Bill, 1999 was introduced in the last session of the 
Parliament. Such a legal framework will facilitate and give a fillip to the e -
commerce activities in the country.

*218. SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any steps are being taken to involve the youth in planning 
process as the Late Prime Minister, Jawahar Lal Nehru, the harbinger of the 
concept of Planning in India considered people's participation as the prime 
sanction being national planning; 
(b) whether there is any scheme to revive Planning Fora in the universities 
and colleges which were higher active at one time; and 
(c) what is the component of the outfit in the Planning Commission to 
ensure integrated publicity to the planning activity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE 
MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Yes, Sir. The involvement of youth in the Planning Process 
is being operationalised through various programmes of Youth Affairs under 
the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports by providing them chance of 
community service and awareness about various social issues etc. Among these 
programmes, National Service Scheme (NSS), Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan 
(NYKS), National Service Volunteer Scheme (NSVS), Assistance to Voluntary 
Organisations in the field of youth and Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of 
Youth Development are important one. 
The brief of some of the programmes is given below:—  
National Service Scheme: National Service Scheme is one of the major 
student youth programme started in 1969 aimed at development of student 
personality through voluntary participation in community service. During 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2000] 
1998-99 NSS had about 15 lakh student volunteers on its roll spread over 189 
universities and senior secondary schools. From its inception, more than 1.52 
crore students from the universities, colleges and institutions of higher learning 
have been benefitted from NSS activities. Due to its overwhelming popularity 
and demand, the scheme has been extended to the students of 2 level in selected 
institutions. It has two types of programmes viz. "Regular Activities" and 
"Special Camping Programme". Regular activities include constructive work 
in adopted villages and slums, blood donation, adult and non-formal education, 
health, nutrition, family welfare, AIDS awareness campaigns, tree plantation 
etc. Under 'Special Camping Programe' a camp of 10 days duration is conducted 
every year in the adopted areas on a specific theme "Youth for Rural 
Reconstruction", "Youth for Special Harmony" etc. 
Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan: It has its district offices in about 500 
districts of the country. Over the year NYKS has become the largest grass routs 
level organisation in Asia-pacific region, catering to the needs of more than 6.4 
million rural female and male youth enrolled through 1.79 lakh village -based 
organisations, named Youth Clubs in the areas covering education, training, 
health awareness, self-employment, financial assistance. Besides this, awareness 
generation and activities for the overall development of the rural communities 
are also being taken in the villages with emphasis on value, vision and voluntary 
action. NYKS has also taken programmes in collaboration with other agencies 
like ""Youth action goal-2000" in U.P. in collaboration with other agencies like 
"Youth action goal-2000" in U.P. in collaboration with UNICEF, Awareness on 
Child Rights and Youth Against AIDS Campaign in the North- Eastern States 
etc. NYKS also organises work camps also involving youth club memebrs in 
project planning and management and to improve the organisational skills of 
youth club memebrs. 
Assistance to Voluntary Organisations in the fields of Youth: The main 
focus of this scheme has been on vocational training programmes to promote 
self-employment of youth. Assistance is also being given for conducting youth 
leadership training program me to promote cadres of young dynamic persons 
who would act as catalysts of social change in the rural areas. 
(b) No, Sir. At present, there is no scheme to revive Planning Forum in the 
Universities and Colleges.

1525. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of

40 

[9 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) An Agreement for cooperation 
in the field of agriculture between the Government of India and the Government 
of Mongolia was signed on 16th September, 1996. The Agreement provides for 
Scientific Technical and Economic cooperation in various areas of agriculture. 
The Agreement also provides for Work Plans to be drawn up by mutual agreement 
containing specific proposals/activities to be taken up for implementation 
under the Agreement. A Work Plan for cooperation in t he field of agriculture 
between the Government of India and the Government of Mongolia was signed 
on 28th January, 2000 for the period 2000—2005. The Work Plan contains 
proposals for exchange of seed samples; exchange of scientific and technical 
information; training of Mongolian Specialists in India and study visits of 
Indian Specialists to Mongolia in various fields of agriculture; setting up direct 
contacts between agricultural research institutions of the two countries, etc. 
Under the Work Plan India would be able to obtain seed samples for cold 
resistant and early maturing wheat, buck —  wheat, barley, cold desert grasses, 
vegetables & fruits, potato varieties, send Indian Specialists to Mongolia to 
study cultivation of cold resistant and early maturing wheat; cultivation of 
soyabean and production of vegetable oils, sheep milk processing; exchange 
scientific and technical information in the field of agriculture, etc.

1537. DR. ALL ADI  P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE

HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): The Indian Council of Agricultural Research

(1) Established 261 Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVK) with the State

organizations (NGO), other educati onal institutions, and a few State

Zonal Agricultural Research Stations (ZARS) to take up the additional 
functions of KVK in 53 districts where there is no KVK, to provide a strong 
linkage between technology generation, assessment and refinement,  and 
dissemination.

Agricultural Technology Information Centres (ATIC) with the selected SAUs 
and ICAR Institutes to provide a single window support system to provide

linkage.

undertake various activities for dissemination of technology to the farmers, 
which include farm advisory services, training of farmers and inservice personnel, 
adaptive trials on farmers' fields, field days, front -line demonstrations, kisan 
melas, workshops, diagnostic services, special campaigns, publication of 
extension literatures and technical support to TV and Radio programmes.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) At the third meeting of the India-Nepal Joint 
Working Group on Border Management held in Ka thmandu from February

1571.    SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: 
SHRI EDUARDO FALERIO: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
78 

[9 March,2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether Government have sought clarifications from the US and other 
principal signatories to CTBT as to how far signing of CTBT is compatible 
with maintenance of Nuclear deterrent by the signatories, if so, with what 
response; 
(b) what are the main reasons for refusal of the US Congress to ratify the 
CTBT; 
 
(c) whether Government have since taken any steps to bring about 
consensus about signing of CTBT amongst different sections of Parliament; 
and 
(d) if so, whether any of the parties have sought clarifications and if so the 
details thereof and the Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI AJITKUMAR PANJA); (a) The Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty 
(CTBT) only prohibits underground explosive nuclear testing; other activities 
relating to development, non -explosive testing, production and s afe 
maintenance of nuclear arsenals are not restricted. Thus the CTBT is entirely 
compatible with the maintenance of a nuclear deterrent by those States which 
have already conducted nuclear tests. The Government's view in this regard is 
shared by the US. 
(b) The two main reservations expressed by the US senators voting against 
the CTBT related to lack of trust in maintaining the integrity of the US nuclear 
weapons stockpile without further explosive testing and doubts regarding the 
verifiability of the Treaty. 
(c) and (d) India's stand on the CTBT was articulated by the Prime Minister 
in the UN General Assembly in September 1998 and in Parliament in December 
1998. This was reiterated by the External Affairs Minister at the UN General 
Assembly in September 1999. The priority of our meeting the country's national 
security concerns having been addressed, the Government believes that we 
now need to convey reassurance to the international community and, in this 
regard, desires to develop a national consensus. The Government is encouraged 
by the constructive response to its efforts to build a consensus on the issue of 
CTBT and intends to pursue this exercise.

Action against corrupt public servants 
1604. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether CVC has been considering to nab corrupt public servants and 
making them liable for prosecution even after retirement; 
(b) if so, whether vigilance officers have been deputed to arrange traps to 
nab the corrupt public servants; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) other stringent steps Government propose to take to ensure that  
Government servants may not indulge into unfair means to earn money? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL 
AND TRAINING AND DEPARTMENT OF PENSION AND PENSIONERS' 
WELFARE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND 
PENSIONS (SHRIMATI VASUNDHRA RAJE):  (a) to (c) A public servant 
continues to be liable for any acts of omission or commission committed by 
him while in service even after his retirement, under the provisions of Prevention 
of Corruption Act, 1988. However, under that Act, traps can be arranged to nab 
the corrupt public servant(s) only by Police Officers. The Prevention of 
Corruption Act does not empower the Vigilance Officers to arrange such traps. 
(d) The punitive actions being taken under the Prevention of Corruption 
Act, 1988 duly supporte d by various Conduct Rules governing the service 
conditions of public servants act as a deterrent against corruption. Moreover, 
the drive against corruption in public services to check malpractices in 
administration and to provide efficient public services is a continuing process. 
The policies formulated in this regard are modified from time to time in order to 
make them more effective and responsive to the changing environment. Some 
of the steps taken by the Government in this regard are as under:— 
1. Spec ial drives are launched by the Central Bureau of Investigation 
from time to time to detect cases of disproportionate assets, to organise 
traps to apprehend public servants while demanding and accepting 
illegal gratification and conduct surprise check at sensitive places. 
109 

 
RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2000] 
2. The Central Vigilance Commission Bill has been introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on 20.12.1999 to confer statutory status on the CVC. The Bill stands 
referred to the Joint Committee of both the Houses of Parliame nt on 
21.12.1999 for consideration and its recommendations. 
3. The Central Vigilance Commission has been vested powers vide Para 3(v) of 
Department of Personnel and Training Resolution No. 371/20/ 99-AVD. III 
dated 4th April, 1999 to exercise superintendence over the vigilance 
administration. The Commission has issued several instructions to reduce 
the scope of corruption such as creating a culture of honesty, greater 
transparency in administration, electronics clearance system and 
computerisation of banks, sensitising the public etc. The Central Vigilance 
Commission has also issued Special Chapters on vigilance management in 
public sector banks and public sector undertakings. 
4. It is proposed to set up the institution of Lok Pal to look into the allegations 
of corruption against high public functionaries. Lok Pal Bill was introduced 
in the Lok Sabha on 3.8.1998 but lapsed on the dissolution of the 12th Lok 
Sabha on 26.4.1999. Steps are being taken to introduce the Bill afresh. 
5. The Government set up a Working Group on 'Right to Information and 
Transparency' in January, 1997 which submitted its report to the 
Government on 21st May, 1997. The report of the Group has been processed 
and a Bill for Freedom of Information has been drafted. The Bill is presently 
under examination for introduction in the Parliament. 
6. Recognising that an important aspect of Preventive Vigilance is to ensure 
transparency in public administration, measures of administrative 
reforms such as introduction of Citizens Charters and setting up of 
Facilitation Centre have been initiated. The review and simplification of 
laws, rules and procedures has also been taken up.

1648. SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Government have taken or proposed to take any measure 
to change the existing guidelines to identify any district as a "Backward' one in 
our country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF

MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) Planning and development of an area and allocation 
of funds for the purpose are primarily the responsibility of the concerned State 
Government. Planning Commission has not identified any district as backward 
per se nor has it prescribed any guidelines to identify any district as backward 
in our country. However, the Central Government supplements the efforts of the

weightage for backwardness in the formula used for distribution of Normal

North Eastern States and Sikkim, they have been categorized as Special 
Category States. Further, a non-lapsable pool of funds has been constituted, out 
of the unspent amount from 10% of the budget of the Central Ministries, which 
was to be earmarked.for these States and this is being allocated on a project -
wise basis.
