THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONM ENT 
AND FORE STS (SHRI BABU L AL MARANDI): (a) to (c) According to the 
Mangrove Atlas of India Published in August 1999 by Space Application Centre 
(Indian Space Research Or gani sati on),  Indian har bour s som e of the best m angr ove 
swam ps in the w orld. These are located in the deltas of rivers such as the G anga,

(b) and (c) For eradicating polio from  the country, the Pulse Polio

throughout the country followed by two additional rounds in eight high risk 
States of Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan, West Bengal 
and Uttar Pradesh. The intensive rounds are spread over 3 -4 days . On the firs t 
day the children are imm unized at the fix ed polio booths and from  2nd day 
onwards team s of health workers go from  house to house to imm unize children 
who m ay be lef t over from  the first day. States have been provided with funds to 
create a wareness through inform ation, education and education efforts and by 
involving the Panchayat m em bers for reaching all children in the age group of 
0— 5 years. In addition, the G overnm ent is also taking steps to im prove the 
routine imm unization programm e (including polio) all over the country.

of a separate Society for Copyright Regulation of Indian Producer s of film s and 
Televis ion (SCRIPT ). This  society has  s et up s pecial wings to fight piracy and

It is  a fact that the World Bank, in its  report titled Averting the Old Age Cris is  
published in 1994, has recomm ended a three pillar system  for Old Age Incom e 
Security, the first pillar consists of G overnm ent provided social security; the 
second pillar consists of m andatory contribution towards social security 
(Privately m anaged but publicly regulated); and the third pillar consists of  
voluntary savings.

Ministry of Rural Developm ent. The second pillar consisting of a m andatory  
pension and provident fund schem e is applicable to onl y around 11 percent of  
the total working population and is basically confined to organized labour and  
Central and State G overnm ent em ployees. Alm ost 89 percent of the workforce 
have no m andatory retirem ent schem e and they have to live on their own  
voluntar y savings.  Dave Committee has recomm ended a voluntary pension  
schem e basically for this large segm ent of the working force.

the fact that Governor holds a Constitutional position. When somebody

his Constitutional responsibility. We are discussing the conduct of the

Government. So far as Article 163 of the Constitution is concerned, it  clearly  
say s that t he Governor has the power to appoint a Chief Minister and on the 
advice of the Chief Minister, he has the power to appoint other Ministers. There 
is no dispute about that. If there is a clear verdict after elections, no disput e 
arises. If one party gets a majority, the job of the Governor becomes very 
easy. He has to ascertain the leader of a majority party and invite him to form  a 
Government. But the problem arises when the Governor has to satisfy himself  
in case there is a fractured mandate. Why are we agitating? Sir, if you look at  
the chronological developments that have taken place in Bihar, you yourself  
would come to a c onclusion that the Governor of Bihar has behaved hastily. 
The election process of the Bihar Legislative Assembly completed on the 27t h 
February. The Notification for composition of the Assembly was issued on 
29th February. On the 1st of March, the leaders of two major parties, i.e. NDA  
and RJD called on the Governor. On 2nd March, the Leader of the RJD had a 
formal discussion with the Leader of the Congress Party. The Congress Party 
did not do well in the Assembly elections. We could get only 23 seat s. On t he 
night of 2nd March, the President of the Bihar PCC communicated to the 
Governor over telephone that the Congress

SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (Pondicherry): Sir, I am much 
obliged that you have allowed this discussion today on the role of Governors 
in the discharge of their con stitutional responsibilities in formation of  
Government s in the States in the light of the recent event s in Bihar. I am 
highly thankful to you for having permitted me to participate in this discussion,  
on behalf of the D.M:K Sir, the D.M.K welcomes the spirit of the resolut ion.  
Actually, the Governors are funct ioning under a remote-controlled system. The 
remote-control is always with the Centre. 
The Governors are dancing to the tunes of the Central Government. 
They are toys and tools in the hands of the Central Government. The 
Governors are joining the chorus of the Central Government. Unfortunatery, 
when the BJP rules at the Centre, the Governors dance to the tunes of the 
BJP. When the Congress Party is ruling at the Centre, the Governors are 
dancing to the  tunes of the Congress Government. So, according to the 
D.M.K, the post of Governor is unwarranted. It is an unnecessary post. 
Articles 153 to 162 of the Indian Constitution should be deleted, omitted and 
annulled. The Governor's post should be abolished. After the Constitution was 
framed, several Governments have been thrown out by Governors, on the 
instigation of Central Government. Recently about two years ago, the U.P. 
Government was dismissed. Shri Murasoli Maran fought in the Parliament for 
the re-installation of that Government. Under those difficult circumstances, the 
D.M.K fought and we were able to get the Government installed. Sir, as far as 
the selection of Chief Ministers is concerned, it should not be left to the 
discretion of the Governor. The  selection of Chief Ministers should be done 
only in the Assemblies. It should not be done in the Chambers of Governors. 
The RajBhawan should not select the Chief Ministers of States. That is the 
stand of the D.M.K and the D.M.K Government. So, the discret ion that has 
been contemplated in the Constitution and that is being exercised by the 
Governors, is arbitrary and it should be put an end to. 
Sir, our leader, Dr. Karunanidhi, Shri Murasoli Maran and other 
leaders presented a resolution before the Sarkaria Commission. I may please 
be permitted to quote from it. 'The office of the Governor is a legacy 
238 

[13 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of the British colonial system. The method of appoint ment of the Governor as 
provided for in our Constitution makes it an anachronism in a democratic set  
up. He is a functionary appointed by, and responsible to, the Central 
Government and as such, he could not be expected to understand the local 
conditions and the political situation. The expenditure incurred on the office of  
the Governor does not seem to square with the socialistic pattern of society. 
The expenditure is a wasteful one, which should well be dispensed with. The 
Supreme Court in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh vs State of Vindhya Pradesh 
(1953) SCR (1188) has held that a Mi nister is an officer subordinate to the 
Governor. Thus, the elected representative of the people in legal theory is 
nothing more than a servant of nominee of the Central Government. The time 
is ripe for doing away with the office of the Governor. 
The executive can be dismissed under the West German system by 
a vote of no-confidence called as the "Constructive Vote of non-confidence".  
Under this provision, the executive cannot be dismissed by a no-confidence 
motion unless it is accompanied by the selection of his successor. A system 
similar to this may be adopted here also.  The Chief Minister will discharge the 
functions at present being attended to by the Governor. If there is any 
interregnum, the Chief Justice of the State will discharge the functions while  
there is no Chief Minister." 
Sir, the Constitution Review Committee has been constituted by the 
Government under the Chairmanship of Shri M.N. Venkatachaliah. I request  
that this Committee should take into consideration what I have suggested and 
frame a C onstitution based on the German Constitution which has totally 
abolished the post of Governor,  and everything is vested in the Council of  
Ministers. As such, I request that the post of Governor should be abolished.  If 
there is no post of Governor, then the re would be no discussion on this issue 
in this august House.

Linesman in Phoney Business 
*262 DR. GOPALRAO VITHALRAO PATIL: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news item 
captioned Linesman in "phoney' business published in the Indian Express 
dated the 4th December, 1999, regarding cheap calls abroad with the help of 
MTNL linesman; and 
(b) if so, what steps are being proposed to avoid such racket? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) and (b) A statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2000] 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The following steps have been taken to prevent recurrence:— 
 
— Prabhadevi Exchange, where the incident took place was of old 
technology (analog type). It has already been replaced by digital 
exchange. 
— Special surveillance is being maintained on such vulnerable 
exchanges. 
— The digital exchanges employ highly sophisticated signaling 
protocols which can not be simulated easily and als o there is no 
possibility for tapping individual junctions. 
— New technology Trunk Automatic Exchanges (Tax) have been 
installed which check the calling line identification and knock 
down the Tax call if it is directly originated from the junction. 
— As a prev entive measure, night inspections of Telephone 
Exchanges arc being conducted by Senior officers apart from 
officers of vigilance unit to check any possible misuse. 
— Dedicated CBI cells have been created in the four metros to detect 
and check telecom related frauds. 
— Strengthening of vigilance cells in ,the field units. 
DR. GOPALRAO VITHALRAO PATIL: Sir, some strange things are 
happening in the Telecom Department. Recently a CBI inquiry was ordered in 
one case. It was found that telephone lines at the Prabhadevi Exchange, which 
is the headquarters of MTNL at Mumbai, were being tapped. The CBI busted 
a racket. The CBI raided the house of a linemen and Rs.24 lakhs were seized 
from his possession. Some such things  are going on. I would like to know 
whether it was a fact and how it happened? 
SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR: Sir, it is a fact that Mr. C. Chandrashekhar, a 
phone mechanic in the Prabhadevi Exchange, Mumbai, has been arrested and 
Rs. 24.3 lakhs have been recovered from his residence alongwith his passport. 
A mobile telephone has also been recovered from his locker in the office. 
DR. GOPALRAO VITHALRAO PATIL: Sir, as we listened to the answer, 
we find that this is a very serious affair. This has a very different dimension. 
Here, 
10 

[14 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the underworld, working from Dubai and Karachi, is also involved. The 
person who had been arrested was hand -in-glove with the underworld, and all 
kinds of calls, whether ISD or STD, were made. The telephone lines had 
bypassed the exchange point and pulse code modulation system of the 
mainline. Ten telephone connection had been provided to these people. The 
Trunk Automatic Exchange was also bypassed. So, such serious things have 
been taking place. It has a security dimension. Terrorists are working against 
the cou ntry. So many things are happening in various cities, including 
Mumbai. I would like to know what steps the Government is taking to prevent 
such things. 
SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR: Yes, Sir, it is a matter of grave concern. Of 
course, these types of cases have been identified in other places also. So far as 
this case is concerned, three telephones, i.e. 4211668,4211670 and 4212831 
which were non-STD and non-ISD, were given ISD and STD facility through 
the Trunk Automatic Exchange by Mr. Chander Shekhar. Mr. Ram Shanker 
Yadav who is TTA has also been identified. Mr. Chander Shekhar is a phone 
mechanic. We have already taken some measures to control these things at the 
Prabha Devi Exchange. This was an old exchange, an analog type of 
exchange. This exchange has already  been upgraded as a modern digital 
exchange. This type of tapping work cannot be done through these modern 
exchanges, especially digital exchanges. This is my assurance to the House. 
Moreover, new technology Trunk Automatic Exchanges (TAX) have been 
installed which check the calling line identification and knock down the TAX 
call if it is directly originated from the junction. With this latest technology 
which is world -class technology, this type of work cannot be done in future. 
We have created more and mo re CBI cells to look into these things. Already, 
on the 9th of this month one man has been identified in Calcutta also. From 
there, Rs. 1,17,54,568 have been recovered. National Savings Certificates and 
other saving certificates worth Rs. 19,05,295 and gol d jewellery worth Rs. 
4,64,477 have been recovered. Sixteen bank accounts in different nationalized 
banks have been freezed. Keys of lockers have yet to be recovered. Bank 
balance of Rs. 3 lakhs and some movable households and other assets have 
already been detected. The CBI is taking stern action against them. I would 
also like to inform the hon. Member of this House that during 1998- 99,154 
Gazetted officers and 245 non -Gazetted officers have been punished on 
several corruption charges. Eleven Gazetted off icers and 42 non- Gazetted 
officers are being prosecuted for criminal misconduct. Besides, 17 Gazetted 
officers and 75 nun -Gazetted officers have been suspended. Similarly, in the 
year 1999-2000. that is, up to 31.1.2000, 130 Gazetted officers and 311 non-  
Gazetted officers have been punished. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA . [14 March, 2000] 
Thirty Gazetted officers and 110 non -Gazetted officers are being prosecuted. 
Twenty Gazetted officers and 111 non -Gazetted officers have been 
suspended. We are taking stern action againstaH these people. But because of 
old technology and because of non- upgraded technology we could not take 
stern action. But at present we are getting more and more latest and world -
class technology. I think we will be able to check these things gradually. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, the hon. Minister has given certain 
figures about telecommunication frauds and the action taken by the 
Government. One of the major reason why these lapses are taking place is 
because of the obsolute technology, as it was in t he Prabha Devi Exchange. I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether he can indicate what has 
been the improvement after CBI cells were entrusted with the job of 
identifying and detecting the telecommunication frauds in the four 
metropolitan cities . He has given some figures in respect of Calcutta. What 
about the other three metropolitan cities —  Delhi, Mumbai and Chennai? If he 
does not have the figures, he can collect it and lay it on the Table of the 
House.

Medical Checkup of Cabin Crew 
1988. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that cabin crew are subjected to annual medical 
checkup without formulating compensation policy in the event of medical 
grounding; and 
(b) if so, whether such medical check-up is against the service rule? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) 
and (b) As per Regulation 47 of Air India Employees se rvice regulations and 
secion 30 (c) and (d) of the standing orders, Female Cabin Crew (Air 
Hostesses) are required to undergo flying duties upto 35 years which may be 
extended to 50 years subject to their medical fitness for this purpose;. They are 
required to undergo biennial Medical examination after they attain 37 years of 
age upto 45 years of age and thereafter they are required to undergo medical 
examination on annual basis till they attain 50 years of age. A separate 
compensation policy in the form of annuity in the event of cabin crew being 
found medically unfit to perform duties of cabin Crew in set out in the 
Memorandum of Settlement of October 1972 signed between Air India and the 
then Air Corporation Employees Union. Male Cabin Crew are not required to 
undergo any corresponding medical examination because from the inception 
of service, the age of retirement of male Cabin Crew was 58 years without any 
question of an extention of service in their case. 
In Indian Airlines , Flying Cabin Crew are retained in the service of the 
Company so long as they remain medically fit for duties but are retired on 
attaining the medical examination once a year after attaining the age of 35 
years. There is also a Provisions for grant of ann uity for medically unfit Cabin 
Crew at variable rates which forms part of the settlement signed with the 
representative Union.

Demand of FICCI for long term fiscal Policy     
2064. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state:

92 

[14 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction to such demand made by FICCI; 
(c) whether Government are aware that long term fiscal policies are 
prevalent in many developed and developing countries;

implementation in the country; and 
(e) if so, the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) In formulating its fiscal policy the Government keeps in view the  
suggestions made by various professional/trade/business organisations. The  
Government recognise the need for imparting predictability in tax policy and  
policies are formulated keeping in view the economic situation and need for  
appropriate balance between revenue and expenditure consistent with policy  
objectives. On the taxation front the basic approach has been to move towards  
a tax structure which is simple, follows sound economic principles, relies on  
moderate tax rates and places emphasis on wider base and better 
enforcement. in Excise the task of convergence to a single rale of 16 per cent 
Central Value Added tax at the centre has been accomplished. This will 
encourage States to  implement their agreed programmes for converting their 
sales taxes into VAT  by 1.4.2001. Customs duty rates are being gradually 
phased down to bring  them broadly in line wit h Asian levels in a few years. 
On the Direct taxes side,  the emphasis has been to retain moderate tax rates 
for corporate and personal  taxes. For medium term management of the fiscal 
deficit a committee has been  set up to examine and make suitable  
recommendations for a strong institutional mechanism embodied in a Fiscal 
Responsibility Act. For expenditure  management and restructuring an 
Expenditure Reforms Commission has been set up. 
(c) to (e) Fiscal policies very considerably across developed and 
developing countries in terms of objectives, target variables, institutional 
coverage and method of implementation. Fiscal policy pursued by a country 
is largely a  function of its assessment of its economy, fiscal situation 
institutional structure and policy objectives.

CALLING ATTENTION TO MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC 
IMPORTANCE 
Situation arising out of mounting non-performing assets of banks 
SHRI GURUDAS DAS GUPTA (West Bengal): Sir, through this 
Calling Attention Notice, I call the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance to 
the situation arising out of the mounting non -performing assets (NPAs) of 
many of the public sector banks and the need for urgent steps for restoration 
of the health of such banks. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, asset class ification and income recognition norms were 
initially     applied    to banking sector in   1992  and banks started asset  
172 

[14 March, 2000]             RAJYA SABHA 
classification and identification of NPAs on objective basis of defaults/record 
of recov ery from 1992- 93. After stabilization of identification norms and 
accounting of NPAs with concerted efforts over the period, the NPAs have 
been coming down in percentage terms. In percentage terms, gross NPAs 
which were 17.84 per cent of the total advances  as on 31.3.1997 have fallen 
to 15.89 per cent of total advances as on 31.3.1999. However, in absolute 
terms, the net NPAs of public sector banks have increased from Rs. 20285 
crore as on 31.3.1997 to Rs. 24211 crore as on 31.3.1999, while declining as 
a percentage of net advances from 9.18 per cent to 8.13 per cent during the 
same period. 
There are a number of factors for an asset turning into non-
performing. Some are internal, namely, wrong selection of project, deficient 
credit appraisal, managerial inef ficiency, lack of supervision by banks/FIs, 
lack of adequate, timely and continued support by the lending institutions and 
in some cases diversion and misutilisation of funds by the borrowers. 
However, a number of NPAs arise on account of external factors such as 
changes in policies, changes in technology rendering some products obsolete 
and some processes relatively costly, environmental concerns leading to 
decisions of Courts on relocation of industrial units and industry level factors 
such as cyclical downturn in some sectors. 
Having regard to the variety of reasons that had led to NPAs, the 
RBI and the Government as well as public sector banks have taken a number 
of steps not only to check the fresh incidence of NPAs but also to ensure the 
recovery of NP As. The steps taken by the Reserve Bank of India, 
Government of India and the public sector banks include the preparation of 
documents of loan recovery policy, reduction through negotiated settlement 
ensuring maximum recovery at minimum cost, strengthening  the Debt 
Recovery Tribunal mechanism, setting up of settlement advisory committee 
and focusing on recoveries by setting up recovery cells at Head Offices. 
In order to strengthen the Debt Recovery mechanism an Ordinance 
has been promulgated on 17.1.2000 to amend the Recovery of Debts due to 
Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993. I may add, as the Secretary -
General has said, that this has been passed by the other House and will be 
coming before this House. The Ordinance provides, inter alia, for set -off and 
counter claims, measures for prevention of alienation of property, 
appointment of receivers and commissioners by the Tribunals, appointment of 
172 

RAJYA SABHA [14 March, 2000] 
more than one recovery officer, and empowering the Tribunals to distribute  
the sale proceeds among secured creditors in accordance with the provisions 
of the Companies Act, 1956. In addition to DRTs and DRATs, which have 
either been set up or at an advanced stage of being set up, I propose to set up 
4 more DRTs in Mumbai and one each in Calcutta, Delhi and Chennai. 
Sharing of credit -related information on borrowers and potential 
borrowers is an input to improvement in credit decisions. A Credit 
Information Bureau to facilitate this is being set up. 
Banks as financial intermediari es are in a business activity that 
necessarily involves risks. The attempt has been, and must continue to be, to 
put in place systems that minimize risk, promote and create productive assets 
and increase profitability and viability of banks. Government is fully 
committed to providing credit support for agriculture, industry and business, 
while fully ensuring the soundness of financial system and good health of 
banks.

alarming. As we are going in for globalisation to compete with the industry at

I will only make one general comment and that general comment is  
let us not see the ghosts where the y don't exist. For everything let us not  
blame the IMF, the World Bank and the WTO. I think it is time to go out of  
this very narrow mindset. There is no reason for a country like India to be  
afraid or scared of any one of these organisations or their memb ership. We

they have gone for ever. Similarly, we all know, the World Bank does not  
dictate the policy. T hey give us some loans because we are members of the  
World Bank. Those are assistances that they give for specific projects. For 
the last  two years there has been some decline in that also because of the  
sanctions. We are aware of that.  
We have discussed  about the WTO in this House. I don't have to  
take the time of the House. As far as the NPAs are concerned, let me make it  
clear that NPAs are not the result of the liberalisation policies which were  
started in this country in 1991. It is not because of li beralisation policy that 
suddenly we have Rs.58,000 crores of NPAs. NPAs have been there from 
before. What happened as a result of the liberalisation policies is that we 
became aware of this fact that we have to look at the health of our financial 
institutions. As I have said in my preliminary speech, the whole concept was

brought to the forefront only in 1992. It was from 1993- 94 that the banks 
were required to start calculating and reporting their NPAs. Before that, there  
could have been NPAs. But we were not even aware of how much NPA was 
there for each bank and what was the prudential norm. Let me say that today, 
we are far more aware and conscious of the need for the absolutely robust 
health of the financial sector because it is the experience of all the countries 
in the world of the global community that a problem will begin, a crisis will 
begin if the financial sector is not up to the mark. What has happened in East -
Asia? The basic problem that took place in East Asia was the weakness of the 
financial sector which could not tackle the crisis, which overtook the 
countries of the region. Therefore, our concern is that our financial sector 
should be absolutely healthy, in the pink of health. It is the prime need of the 
hour. There is no way this country can afford to let the things drift. Therefore, 
we have to do the prudential norms prescribed by the Central Bank, by the 
Reserve Bank of India which compare with the best in the world.And we are 
proud of the fact that we hav e now norms which are much better than most 
developed countries also. We are continuously improving upon those 
prudential norms year after year so that, as I said, we can bring the financial 
sector to the pink of health.

intention to conceal any figure from the House. But the fact is that ever since 
we started on this in 1993- 94, as a result of the steps taken by succeeding 
Governments, NPAs both in the gross and net terms, have been going down.

decline. I am saying, it is as a result of the efforts made by succeeding

are aware of the fact that in our context, we have a norm of something like 
four per cent. It will be our endeavour to take effective steps so that we can

owners and we want to recapitalize. We are in need of recapitalisation.' And I

money today because I don't have the money to give. Therefore, how do the 
banks recapitalise? In the given situation, either we allow the banks to go sick,

shareholding will be brought down below 50 per cent, and because of  this 
fact, the rest of the shares will not be strategically held by any other party.

Percentage of armed recruits from Orissa 
*282. MISS FRIDA TOPNO: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the percentage of recruitment in armed forces from Orissa is 
less as compared to other States; 
(b) the number of recruitment centres of Army, Navy and Air Force 
separately in Orissa; and 
(c) the reasons for less recruitment from Orissa and the remedial steps 
proposed for it? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
The recruitment of Sailors in Navy and Airmen in Air Force is carried out 
on the basis of all-India merit and no specific quota is allotted to any particular 
State. Therefore, no comparison can be drawn with respect to recruitment to 
these forces from different States. 
The recruitment of Jawans in Army is based on allocation of vacancies to 
States. Distribution of 'all -India all class vacancies' of Army among States is 
done on the basis of their Recruitable Male Population (RMP). The RMP is that 
proportion of the male population, which meets the laid down age limits and 
minimum standards of education for enrolment to Army. This is expressed as a 
percentage of the total Male Population (TMP). This method of allocation of 
vacancies among the States/UTs ensures that each State gets its due and 
equitable share of vacancies available in a year in Army. The RMP of Orissa is 
3.66 per cent which is more than that of 21 States/Union Territories. 
As the States have different allocation of vacancies because of variation 
in population, State -wise recruitment to Army generally conforms to the 
allocation profile.

the last three years was as under:

16 

{15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
STATEMENT 
(a) Yes, Sir. The textile account for approximately l/3rd of our total exports. 
(b) In 1997-98, the textile exports grew in dollar terms by 4.2% compared to 1996-
97 while in 1996-97 the same grew by 10.8% compared to 1995-96. 
(c) The main reasons for decline are:—  
(i) Slow growth in cotton yarn exports due to slowdown in South East Asian 
economy. 
(ii) Low unit value realisation in non-restrained items in the case of apparel 
articles. 
(iii) Non-release of exceptional flexibilities in full by EU during 1997. 
(iv) General recession in the world market (there was overall decline in 
Indian exports by 2%). 
(d) Government have been taking several steps from time to time to 
boost textile exports. Some of the important initiatives are as under:— 
(1) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme has been made 
operational with effect from 1 -4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation 
and Upgradation of textile sector. 
(2) The New Export Entitlement (Quote) Policy for the period 2000— 2004 
has been announced to provide stability and continuity and encourage 
competitiveness in textile exports. 
(3) Non-Quota Entitlement (NQE) System for encouraging Non-Quota exports 
to Quota and non-quota countries has been retained* to boost exports 
in apparel sector-value added segment of Indian textiles. 
(4) Threshold limit under the Zero Duty Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) 
Scheme has been reduced to Rs. 1 crore in respect of certain prescribed 
textile machinery. 
(5) Exports of cotton yarn by Export Oriented Unit (EOU)/Export 
Promotion Zone (EPZ)/EPCG units has been liberalised. 
(6) Zero Duty import of certain categories of trimmings & 
embellishments has been allowed.

Purchase of Residential Plots in Himachal Pradesh 
*287. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Central Government employees are not allowed 
to purchase residential plots in the State of Himachal Pradesh; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government would contemplate a policy decision allowing 
the Central Government employees to purchase residential plots in Himachal 
Pradesh; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) to (d) 
According to information received from the Government of Himachal Pradesh, 
section 118 of the Himachal Pradesh Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1972 
provides that non- agriculturists cannot purchase land without the permission 
of the State Government for the prescribed purpose. The word agriculturist has 
been defined under section 2 of the said A ct as a person who cultivates land 
personally in an estate situated in Himachal Pradesh. Therefore, a Central 
Government employee, who is an agriculturist under the provisions of the Act, 
can purchase land in his name. However, if he is not an agriculturis t, he can 
purchase land in Himachal Pradesh only with the prior permission of the State 
Government. Besides, a non -agriculturist can purchase land/built up house 
from the Himachal Pradesh State Housing Board and Development Authority 
without the permission of the State Government. A non- agriculturist can also 
purchase land within the Municipal areas without permission in case he was 
residing in Himachal Pradesh on the commencement of the Act, i.e., 21.2.1974.

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) to (c) No 
Statewise record regarding the number of security and police personnel killed in 
landmine blasts, is maintained by the Central Government. However, the 
Government of India and the concerned State Governments continuously review 
the situation arising out of militancy, terrorism,  insurgency and extremist 
activities. 
In order to tackle cross-border terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir, Government 
of India has implemented an action plan. For neutralising militancy/terrorism 
in the North- East various steps including deployment of CPMFs and A rmy, 
improved coordination and intelligence sharing between security forces, 
modernisation/upgradation of State Police Forces etc. have been undertaken. 
For effectively countering Left Wing Extremism, the affected States of 
Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Orissa were requested 
to prepare integrated action plans encompassing the development as well as 
security aspects of the problem for the affected areas. The States have also been 
advised to take vigorous follow -up action. The Governm ent of India has also 
set up a coordination centre headed by the Union Home Secretary with Chief 
Secretaries and Directors General of Police of the States affected by Left Wing 
Extremism, as its members, to review steps taken to check the Left Wing Extremist 
activities, monitor the plan of action in respect of each state etc. 
In addition, in order to minimise attacks due to landmine and/or IED 
blasts on security forces/police personnel/civilians, steps such as deployment 
of road opening parties, use of metal detectors, mine protected vehicles etc. 
are being taken.

(a) whether it is a fact that ammunition worth Rs. 11.84 crore imported 
against doubtful certificate of inspection from Pitcare Ltd. Hongkong in January, 
1993, was subsequently rejected as it failed in a test check in Central 
Ammunition Depot, Pulgaon;

A contract dated 21.1.1993 was singed with M/s Pitcare Ltd. Hongkong for 
supply of 10000 rounds of 130mm and 6700 rounds of 122mm illuminating 
ammunition for an amount of USD 6.12 million. The Ce ntral Ammunition 
Depot (CAD), Pulgaon intimated in September 1993 the receipt of consignment 
of 10000 nos of 130mm Illuminating ammunition from Hongkong against the 
contract. Since the consignment was received without technical literature and 
range tables, the check proof was delayed. The check proof was conducted in 
August 1995 on receipt of fuze setting key and range tables from the firm. Ten 
rounds were fired and three recorded defects. The consignment was subjected 
to reproof by firing 13 rounds in Dece mber, 1995 out of which 12 recorded 
failures.

check proof, the consignment was recommended as "Not fit for Use" hand 
quality claim raised.

Agreement to make Bofors Gun in India 
2143! SHRI VAYALWR RAVI: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government made an agreement to make the Bofors gun in 
India; 
(b) whether Government made any negotiation for advance technology for 
the gun production; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to (c) A 
contract dated 24.3.1986 was concluded with M/s A.B. Bofors, Sweden for 
procurement of 410 nos. of 155mm FH 77B Gun System with accessories and 
ammunition. In addition, a license agreement was also concluded on the same date 
with the said company for the license manufacture of the systems in India. 
The Gun Systems under the supply contract were received and introduced in 
service. However, before indigenous production could be launched, there were 
certain allegations regarding illegitimate payments to various persons. Thereupon, 
on 31.1.1990 it was decided that no further steps will be taken to operationalise the 
license production agreement until Borors reveals the names and full details of 
recipients and returns the amounts paid. 
In June, 1999, the ban placed on M/s A.B. Bofors in the light of the 
impact and the changed situation, was re-examined and it was decided that without 
prejudice to the ongoing investigations, actions due and reserving to Government the 
right to be reimbursed amounts illegitimately paid, the embargo placed on M/s Bofors 
need not visit the successor company, the present Celsius of Sweden which is state 
controlled and unconnected with institutions that owned M/s A.B. Bofors. 
No final decision has yet been taken by the Government regarding the 
155mm 45 calibre gun offered by M/s Celsius for trials in May, 2000 nor any 
negotiation held with the company.

DR. D. MASTHAN: 
Will the Minister of MINES AND MINERALS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that indigenous coal would become costly in 
comparison to the imported coal in the southern States of the country due to the 
decision taken by the Ministry of Railways for hiking the freight on coal; 
(b) if not, what is the assessment made by Government in this regard; and

departments for checking the import of coal, and if so, the details thereof?

MINERALS (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) to (c) The indigenous coal per

Governments that any further increase in railway freight and the royalty rates would 
make Indian coal further uncompetitive.

However, the States which have undertaken restructuring have reported T&D 
losses varying from 40 to 51%. The loss can be classifi ed under two broad 
categories; namely, technical loss and commercial loss. The technical losses 
are inherent in the system and can be reduced by better design of lines, relocation 
of distribution transformers and installation of capacitors. The Commercial 
losses are due to theft of energy, use of defective meters and un-metered supply. 
The losses due to theft and pilferage of energy are presently camouflaged under 
T&D losses.

(c) The Central Electricity Authority had issued comprehensive guidelines 
in July, 1991 to the SEBs and Electricity Department for reduction of T&D 
losses. The commercial losses including theft of energy can be effectively 
prevented by energy auditing at sub-station level, electronic and remote control

Power Crisis in the Ensuing Summer 
2233. DR. MOHAN BABU: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a worst power crisis all over the country is 
anticipated in the ensuing summer; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the action taken by Government to avert the crisis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Based on the tentative generation target and 
anticipated requirement of energy in various regions of the country during the 
ensuing summer months of April/May and June, 2000, the country is likely to 
face energy shortage of the order of 5.5%. The energy shortage in Northern, 
Southern and Western Regions are likely to be of the order of 7.1 % 6.8% and 
4.4% respectively. Eastern and North -Eastern Regions are not likely  to face 
any energy shortages. 
(b) The reasons for shortage of power are greater increase in requirement 
of energy compared to availability, low voltage conditions in the grid due to 
inadequate installation of shunt capacitors, shortage of peaking power in the  
grid, constraints in transmission and distribution system and low PLF of some 
of the power station. 
(c) In order to improve availability of power and generation capacity and 
make optimal use of the available power resources in the country, the following 
measures have been taken:—  
(i) Expeditious implementation of capacity addition programme. 
(ii) Promotion of measures for demand side management such as flattening 
of load curve by staggering weekly off day of industrial consumers 
and regulation of power supply to consumers through grouping 
restrictions. 
(iii) Renovation and modernisation(R&M) of existing generating stations. 
(iv) Disbursement of loans by Power Finance Corporation for improving 
operation and maintenance of thermal power stations under accelerated 
generation programme. 
(v) Promotion of inter-state and inter-regional power transfers. 
118 

[15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) Coordinated operation of hydro, thermal nuclear and gas turbine power 
stations in the regional power system. 
(vii) Augmentation of transmission, transformation capacity in the power 
system and installation of shunt capacitors to improve the voltage. 
(viii) Reduction of transmission and distribution losses.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI

pilferage and technical losses.

Statement-III 
Resolution of the Chief Ministers/Power Ministers Conference Held on 
26.02.2000 
The Power Ministers' Conferen ce took note of the impending difficult 
situation facing the power supply industry in the country due to continuing 
decline in commercial viability of the sector as a whole. It noted the fact that:— 
1. Outstanding dues of CPSUs have been increasing and have now reached 
Rs. 23,000 crores. This trend if maintained would adversely affect 
their current operations apart from their future expansion plans. 
2. Financial closure for private power projects is becoming increasingly 
difficult. 
3. The states are unable to finance new projects on their own. 
4. Increases in budgetary support from state governments as well as central 
government for this sector is not feasible due to fiscal deficits. 
II. The primary factors responsible for this unsustainable financial 
situation are:    
(i) Theft and pilferage at the macro level are estimated to be over Rs. 
20,000 crores per annum. 
(ii) Technical losses in transmission & distribution for the country are 
also too high. 
128 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) Large number of the thermal stations in the State sector run at an 
operational efficiency of less than 40%. 
(iv) The average annual operational losses of the State Power Sector for the 
country is over as. 12,000 crores. 
III. It was also recognised that the cross subsidies cannot be sus tained if 
industrial tariffs make Industry non -competitive in the new environment of 
increasing globalisation with elimination of quantitative and other restrictions. It 
becomes necessary to ensure that Indian Industry is not handicapped by 
unsatisfactory power supply or by tariff which makes it non-competitive. Further, the 
consumer, including the fanner has a legitimate claim for uninterrupted good 
quality power supply. His willingness to pay reasonable costs is 
underestimated. 
Resolutions 
1. The Power Mi nisters' resolved after taking into account all the  
problems facing the power sector, that with the intention of achieving 
commercial viability and providing power at reasonable rate to all,  
reform must be undertaken with determination, vigor and a sense o f 
urgency. Delay in reform only increases the financial cost of reforms, 
and the burden of liabilities only increases. Reforms must begin to  
show results within the next 2-3 years. The key elements of the reform 
strategy are:—  
(a) Energy Audit at all levels. 
(b) Time-bound programme of 100% metering of all consumers by 
December 2001. 
(c) Reduction and finally, elimination of power theft within a specified 
time frame. 
(d) Strengthening/upgradation of sub -transmission and distribution 
system by taking sub-station as an unit on a priority basis. 
 
2. If the above appears unattainable in the existing set up corporatisation/ 
cooperatization/privatization of distributions, would have to be 
undertaken. 
3. Since a large number of thermal stations within the State sector are 
running at a P LF below 40% immediate Renovation & Modernisation 
including Life Extension would need to be undertaken on an urgent 
 129 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
basis. Similarly, R&M/LE would require to be undertaken for old 
hydel power plants on priority. 
4. Effective functioning of State Electricity Regulatory Commissions is 
essential for rationalization of tariff, and balancing the interests of the 
consumer and the need for commercial viability of the utilities in the 
environment where private sector participation in the industry is 
expected to gradually increase. 
5. Unbundling and corporatization of State Electricity Boards/ bench-
marking through separate distribution profit centres/corporations/ 
companies may facilitate the Regulatory Commissions in prom- oting 
competition within the power supply industry —competition being 
the key to lower prices. 
6. It was noted that the power system network in country has an unmatched 
reach to consumers and with the installation of optic fibre cables 
along the existing power lines using its right of way, it has the potential 
of generating very large resources in the coming years by providing 
facilities for multipurpose communication including cable TV, IT 
services, Telecom services, etc. Hence efforts need to be made to 
creatively tap this potential source of large revenue from convergence. 
7. In order to promote reforms, a new draft central legislation which 
obviates the need for separate enactments for the States, is being 
considered. The draft Bill submitted by the NCAER would form the 
basis for a national debate and a consensus on the contents of the new 
Bill. The States would be sending their detailed comments on this 
draft Bill, to the Ministry of Power at the earliest.

Study on India's Power Policies by World Bank 
2244. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the attention of the Government has been drawn to the news 
item captioned ""Government rejects WB study on India's power policies" as  
reported in the Times of India dated 29th December, 1999; 
(b) whether the World Bank is interested to conduct study on India's  
power sector policies; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) the details of guidelines issued by the World Bank during the past 
three years with regard to India's power policies; and 
(e) to what extent Government have implemented them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir. The Government is aware of the news item 
which states that the Government rejects World Bank study on India's power 
policies. The Government does not agr ee with the conclusion sought to be 
projected in the document of the World Bank since the entire document is 
based on the basis of some studies conducted in only two states,"viz. Bihar and 
Andhra Pradesh. The per capita emission of carbon-di-oxide in India is between 
one tenth to one twentieth of the per capita carbon -di- oxide emission in 
developed countries. Besides, all power plants in India are established after 
obtaining full environmental clearance. The Government is also committed to 
promoting effici ency. The use of efficient generating plants and pollution 
control technologies is bound to reduce the level of emissions. The efforts of 
energy conservation including demand side management will also reduce 
demand. The Fly Ash Mission is doing extensive w ork on optimum flyash 
utilisation. The Government is also aware of the financial problems of the State 
Electricity Boards which is the other aspect referred to in the World Bank 
document. The Government has, consequently, focussed on the issue of reforms 
over the last two years. 
(b) No proposal has been received from the World Bank for conducting a 
study on India's power sector policies. 
(c) Does not arise. 
(d) and (e) The World Bank does not issue any guidelines in regard to 
India's power sector policies. They generally lay down covenants at the time of 
138 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
signing the loan agreements with the operating/project implementing agencies 
for grant of loan for a particular power project/scheme. The Bank has its own 
internal operational procedures, policies and guidelines.

Transmission and distribution losses of power 
2249. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to  
state: 
(a) whether Government have made any assessment of the loss of Power 
during transmission and distribution during a year; 
(b) whether power loss has been on the rise with every passing year; 
(c) the estimated power loss from 1998 to 1999; 
(d) whether significant part of the transmission and distribution losses 
are due to pilferage; and 
(e) if so, the measures taken or proposed to be taken through out the 
country to check these transmission and distribution losses? 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The figures of tran smission arid 
distribution losses for the year 1998-99 are not yet available. According to the 
figures reported by SEBs/EDs/ Power Utilities, the T&D losses during the year 
1996-97 and 1997-98 on all India basis were 24.53% and 24.44% (tentative) 
respectively. However, the States which have undertaken restructuring have 
reported T&D losses varying from 40 to 51%. 
(d) The losses can be classified under two broad categories, namely, 
technical loss and commercial loss. The technical losses are inherent in the 
system and can be reduced by better design of lines, relocation of distribution 
transformers and installation of capacitors. The commercial losses are due to 
theft of energy, use of defective meters and unmetered supply. The losses due to 
theft and pilferage are presently, camouflaged under T&D losses. 
(e) In order to reduce the transmission & distribution losses, the Central 
Electricity Authority has issued comprehensive guidelines in July 1991, which, 
inter-alia provide for the following; 
 
— Up gradation of operating voltages; 
— Reducation of length of LT lines; 
— Location of transformers near load centres; 
— Adoption of low capacity transformers near consumers' pre- mises; 
— Installation of shunt capacitors; 
— Improvement in construction and operation techniques; and 
— Systematic and methodological approach for planning and design of 
distribution system on a long term basis. 
— Conducting energy audit and providing a methodology for segregating 
technical and commercial losses. 
Necessary amendments have been made in the Indian Elec tricity Act, 
1910, to make the theft of electricity a cognizable offence. 
Under the Accelerated Power Development Programme, it is proposed to 
provide funds to the State Governments for implement- ing specific projects for 
improving the sub-transmission and distribu- tion system including installation 
of state-of-the-art electronic meter- ing system. 
In the Conference of Power Ministers' which was held on 26.2.2000, the 
State/UT Governments have resolved to undertake energy auditing at all levels 
142 

[15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
and to install meters for all consumers by December, 2001. With the adoption of 
these measures, it will be possible to substantially reduce losses arising due to 
power thefts.

2251. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state:

stations in the country for more than ten years; and

statutory benefits? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) does 
not keep the record of Contract Labour engaged by the contractor to whom 
NTPC has awarded the contract to carry out specific jobs. After a contract is 
awarded for carrying out certain jobs, contractor deployes the requisite workmen 
for carrying out the job. As and when the job is over or contract expires, the 
Contract Labour are redeployed/disengaged by the Contractor. NTPC has no 
role to play except to ensure that contractor meets all the statutory requirements 
like payment of wages, leave, holidays etc. 
(b) All contractors who are awarded contract by NTPC are extending all 
statutory benefits to their employees. In addition, NTPC ensures the same by 
the following mechanism: 
— Contract documents contain stipulation that it is obligatory on 
contractor to extend all statutory dues/benefits to his/her employees. 
— Periodical inspection is carried out by NTPC executives to ensure the 
same. 
— If any violation is found or reported, it is promptly rectified.

Suspension of Operations Against Bodo Liberation Tigers 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, thi s august House is aware of the history of militancy in 
Assam.  The activities of various militant groups in the State have seriously  
190

disturbed the public order resulting in loss of life and property, besides 
thwarting the economic development of the State. The people are fed up with 
violence and yearn for peace. The Government of India is committed to the 
restoration of peace. The Government of India has also extended an 
invitation to all the militant groups to come forwar d for talks within the four 
corners of our Constitution. In pursuance - of the said offer, the Bodo 
Liberation Tigers (BLT) have suspended its operations against the Army, 
Para-Military Forces and the State Police. The BLT has also agreed to 
completely abju re the path of violence in both letter and spirit and not to 
indulge in any unlawful activities in case the Government of India announces 
suspension of operations against it. 
In order to create an environment conducive to talks for finding a 
solution to th e Bodo problem, the Government has decided to suspend 
operations against the BLT with immediate effect. 
Effort are continuing to convince other militant groups in the  
North-East to suspend their violent and unlawful activities and come to the  
negotiating table. , 
Incident of Caste Violence in Kolar District 
of Karnataka on 11th March, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Sir, 
yesterday in this House a mention was made of the violent incidents in Kolar 
district of Karnataka. In that connection, it was stated that the Home Ministry 
should obtain the facts and come to the House. We ascertained the facts from 
the State Government and on that basis I make the following statement. 
As per information available with the Central Government, two 
incidents of violence and counter -violence between members of the Reddy 
community and the Scheduled Castes have been taken place in village 
Kambalapalli of Police Station Kencharlahaili in the District of Kolar, 
Karnataka. The incidents resulted in the stabbing  and subsequent death of 
one Krishna Reddy and burning alive of seven members of the Scheduled 
Caste community. 
The sequence of events reveals that on 11th March around 7.30 P.M. 
a group of 15-20 persons belonging to the Scheduled Caste community which. 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
reportedly included two persons named Anjanappa and Sriramappa, stabbed 
one Krishna Reddy who died on the spot. In retaliation a group of 150 -200 
persons belonging to the Reddy community attacked the colony of the village 
inhabited by the Scheduled Caste community around 9.00 P.M. and set fire to 
the house belonging to Sriramappa and another adjoining house. Six persons, 
four men and two women, died on the spot due to suffocation and burn 
injuries and one lady succumbed to her injuries later on the way to hospital. 
The immediate provocation for the murder of Krishna Reddy is 
reported to be a verbal altercation between the Reddys and the Scheduled 
Castes on 9th March on some trivial issue. 
The State Police have arrested 15 pers ons in connection with the 
violence so far. Additional police force has also been stationed at the village 
as well as at the Divisional Headquarters at Chintamani and at District 
Headquarters, Kolar. Prohibitory orders have been enforced at Chintamani 
and Kambalapalli areas since 13th March, 2000. Investigations are on and 
senior police officials are supervising the investigation. The State Chief 
Minister, the State Home Minister and other leaders have visited the spot and 
assured protection to the remainin g Scheduled Caste families and arranged 
relief operations. The Chief Minister has announced institution of a judicial 
inquiry into the incident. The Chief Minister has also announced ex gratia 
compensation of Rs. 1 lakh to each, suitable employment to the next of kin of 
those killed, rehabilitation of the affected people and assured stringent action 
against those who were responsible for the heinous crimes. 
The situation is currently reported to be tense but under control. MR.

Need to Take Effective Measures to Stop Decline of 
Vishwa Bharati Central University 
SHRI GURUDAS DAS GUPTA (West Bengal): Thank you, Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, for allowing me to raise this Special Mention. Sir, I would  like 
to say that Vishwa Bharati, a Central University of the Government of India, 
situated in Bholpur, Shantiniketan, dedicated to the sacred memory of of Dr. 
Rabindra Nath Tagore, seems to be in a process of decline. It has, instead of 
remaining as a Cen tral University - just like any other Central University - 
almost become a local university because of certain corroding problems. 
Students from other parts of the country do not opt for admission to this 
University. There is a serious erosion of academic atmosphere. There is almost 
a breakdown of administration. Key posts in the University are lying vacant. 
Only ad hoc appointments are being made. Generally, the Council does not 
meet. The emergency powers of the Vice- Chancellor, which used to be rarely 
invoked during the earlier period, are now being persistently invoked. The 
person who is the head of the Administration is acting through remote control, 
keeping himself away from the place of his work. Sir, the copyright of Vishwa 
Bharati to Tagore's works h ad expired a few years back that time, Shri 
Narasimha Raoji was the Prime Minister. Many Members of Parliament from 
West Bengal, irrespective of political colour, had prevailed upon the then 
Government to extend the copyright to Vishwa Bharati for a decade, on the 
specific assurance that the Vishwa Bharati University will seek to bring out a 
translated version of Tagore's works in different languages. Sir, I am sorry to 
say that nothing has been done in this regard. Some of the leading citizens of 
West Bengal, belonging to different categories of life, had collectively written 
a letter to the visitor of the University, Rashtrapatiji, and they have also 
addressed a letter to Dr. Murli Manohar Joshiji. 
The leading persons who have sought to seek the intervention of the 
194  

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Government include Smt. Mahasweta Devi, a leading writer, Shri K.G. 
Subramanyam, a well known person, Shri Supriyo Tagore, Shri Somnath 
Here, a leading sculpture and Shri Amlan Dutta, a former Vice -Chancellor. 
There are many other names. They have sent a copy of this letter to me and 
also to Comrade Somnath Chatterjee, Ms. Mamata Banerjee and Shri Tapan 
Sikdar. 1 would like to quote a very small part of the letter. It says , "The 
university has a big body of gar dening staff, but its gardens are some of the 
worst kept in any educational campus. It has a huge battery of watch and 
ward staff, but they are unable to stop the theft of the university property and 
the misuse of its precincts and vandalisation by anti- socials. It has a big 
Maintenance Department that lets its valuable (and historical important) 
buildings go to seed and is unable to prevent damage to its  art treasurers."  
The Government of West Bengal had placed an order for a number 
of replicas of sculptu res of leading artists who had been working in the 
Vishwa Bharati University. Money had been sent by the Government of West 
Bengal but the work has not been done. The money has been diverted for 
some other purpose. This is not all. The important point is, the academic 
career has reached the lowest bottom. An important professor had been made 
to resign. There had been an occasion when in a particular examination 
students were given 99 per cent marks. I am told that teaching there has been 
affected very serio usly. Vandalism is going on. Students have their own 
complaints. Hostels are not properly equipped. The Government of India is 
spending quite a large sum on this university. I am raising this issue not to 
malign the great university dedicated to the memory  of Tagore. I am raising 
this issue because I think that time has come when immediate steps need to be 
taken by the Government of India in consultation with the State Government 
to bring it back to health. Otherwise, it will be a colossal loss to India and  to 
our academic life and we shall be, in a way, maligning the memory of the 
great Tagore. It is the responsibility of the Government of India to protect this 
university. I suggest that an immediate inquiry should be conducted. There 
can be a Parliamentary Committee or it can be left to the Government to take 
steps in consultation with the Government of West Bengal. I would like to 
add a few more words. The persons who have collectively written to the 
Visitor and to the Minister of Human Resource Developmen t, have not given 
the full truth. There are still more things. Sir, I don't want to take much time 
of the House. I only say that this is a national humiliation. This is a national 
dishonour.   This is a national calamity.  This university must be protected .

epitome of training of culture to people who are having an aptitude for 
culture. This is a great cultural institution. 1 beg that the House may kindly 
take note of the serious situation and ask the Government to take immediate 
remedial steps. Thank you.

Non-Availability of Crop Loans in Orissa 
SHRI SANATAN BISI (Orissa): Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. The 
non-availability of crop loans in Orissa is a serious matter. The poor 
cultivators in Orissa are suffering from untold miseries due to non -availability 
of crop loans in time. The commercial banks, including the State Bank of 
India, have not released the crop loans to cultivators although they were 
assured by bank officials on several occasions. The cultivators were expecting 
long-term loans from banks due to the super-cyclone in Orissa but to no avail. 
The issue of Kisan Credit Cards is also not satisfactory. I urge upon the 
Central Government to conduct a high -level inquiry regarding the non -
availability of crop loans in Orissa and to grant early relief to the cultivators.  
Thank you, Sir.

Urgent Need for Transit Facilities for North-East States Through 
Bangladesh, the Area Beinga Landlocked Region 
SHRI KHAGEN DAS (Tripura) : Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, I thank 
you for giving me an oppor tunity to raise the important issue of transit 
facilities to the land-locked North-East through Bangladesh for transportation 
of goods, materials and passengers. 
It is well known that even after 52 years of Independence, the 
North-East remains vulnerably p laced in terms of communication facilities. 
The entire North -East has to depend on just a small corridor through Assam 
which is called the Chicken's neck. The failure in developing appropriate 
transport and communication routes to the North -East is one of the most 
important reasons behind this region's under -development. Although the 
North-East region has a very large stock of oil and natural gas and other 
industrial raw materials, it has not been possible to utilise these natural 
resources for setting up o f industries, due to the transportation problems -  a 
halting hurdle for economic progress. 
It may be mentioned that before the partition of India, trade, traffic 
movement and communication of most of the North-East were linked with the 
plain lands of Briti sh India, now in Bangladesh. Immediately after 
Independence and partition of the country the traditional communication link 
through Bangladesh got snapped. 
I will specifically like to mention about the difficulties people have 
to face in my own State Tripura due to communication problems. 
The distance between Agartala and Calcutta through Bangladesh is 
not more than 400 kms. through the surface route. The aerial distance 
between Agartala and Calcutta is 350 kms. Compared to this, the rail -cum-
road distance from Agartala to Calcutta through Assam is 1,500 kms. The 
present rail -cum-road route passes through jungles, and many times, due to 
heavy rains, this route is blocked. 
It is against this background that the North- Eastern States have been 
requesting the Go vernment of India to take up this matter with the 
Government of Bangladesh so that transit facilities for Indian goods and 
passengers through Bangladesh could be available. The Chief Ministers of the 
North-Eastern States in a meeting at Guwahati last year also raised the 
demand.   A large section of Bangladesh trade community and intellectuals 
212 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
favour the extension of the transit facility and direct communication with the 
North-Eastern States. There were series of exchanges  of visits of trade 
delegations and cultural teams from the North -Eastern States and Bangladesh 
during the last three years. Hence, there is the crying need of transit facility 
through Bangladesh for all the States in the North-Eastern region. 
It may be me ntioned that the Tripura Legislative Assembly has 
unanimously passed a Resolution in its last session, urging the Central 
Government to quicken the talks with Dhaka for a transit route through 
Bangladesh. 
The direct bus service between Dhaka and Calcutta i s a milestone in 
improving the bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh. The opening 
of the direct bus service between Calcutta and Dhaka raises a ray of hope for 
a similar facility in the minds of the people of the North -Eastern region, 
particularly Tripura. The people of Tripura and all other North -Eastern States 
expect and hope that the opening of the bus service, a transit route from 
Agartala to Calcutta via Bangladesh will soon materialise, with the initiative 
of the Government of India and co- operation of the Government of 
Bangladesh, in the interest of the economic development of the region as well 
as mutual benefit of the people of the subcontinent as a whole. 
Thank you, Sir. 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): Sir, with your permission, I want to say that I am in sympathy with 
this requirement and demand. As the hon. Member already knows, this 
Government has already acted in this regard. After all, the opening of the 
land route between Calcutta and Dhaka and the bus journey is the first step 
that was taken for opening up trade transit through Bangladesh. We are in 
negotiation with the Bangladesh Government in this regard. 
The second aspect of the land route, as the hon. Member, no doubt, 
knows, is that we have already an agr eement, in principle, on connecting 
Dhaka with Agartala, through a bypass. That has also been agreed to. It is 
only a small portion of the road track, the road near Akhaura that has fallen 
into disuse. We have very purposely tried to have that restored. We have also 
spoken to the Government of Bangladesh. It is not simply about the land 
route. The agreement in principle is for a multi -model transport arrangement. 
These are the steps in that direction. I can assure you that the Government is 
already acting in this regard.

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
STATUTORY RESOLUTION 
I. Seeking     Disapproval     of the  Telecom   Regulatory 
Authority of India (Amendment) Ordinance, 2000. 
II. The    Telecom     Regulatory    Authority    of    India 
(Amendment) Bill,, 2000. 
SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, I 
move that: 
'that this House disapproves of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of 
India (Amendment) Ordinance, 2000 (No.2 of 2000) promulgated by 
the President on the 24th January, 2000.' 
Sir, I speak with great anguish that the TRAI Ordinance was 
promulgated in utmost haste. One fails to understand, when there was a 
period of just three weeks or four weeks, an d Parliament was to be called, 
when both the Houses were to meet, why such an undue haste was shown, or 
why this step was taken. Sir, there are a few questions which demand 
immediate answer from the Government of India. The Ordinance was 
promulgated to rem ove the existing TRAI. Sir, a long time has passed and 
the Government has failed even to appoint all members for the TRAI. A few 
members were appointed, but not all. Now, Sir, I am quoting from Tribune, 
an English daily from Chandigarh : "The throttling mo nopoly of the DoT and 
the MTNL in two metropolitan cities and finally, the enthusiasm of the 
bureaucrats to retain their horses in power, India's tryst with wrong number is 
going to be long." 
Though MNCs have supported the Ordinance, by and large, the 
common users have not supported it. The overhauling of TRAI should have 
been done after adequate discussions. Sir, no time has been given to the 
representatives of the people, who are sitting here, to discuss the functioning 
of TRAI, its drawbacks and the need  for its further improvement. For 
instance, a serious doubt is prevailing in the mind of the common, man. We 
are aware of the functioning of the Government. All  important opinion-
makers have given their views. They say that when the session was just three  
weeks away, the Government should not have issued such an Ordinance. 
Obviously, there was pressure from certain quarters. What were the 
compulsions before the Government? Which were the lobbies involved in it 
which compelled the Government to take such a hasty decision? 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
The country wants to know it. The Government must come out in 
the open. The loss of revenue suffered by the Government amounts to Rs.300 
crores. The Government has suffered this loss because they had deci ded to do 
away with the licence fee and to go in for revenue sharing. These things 
should have been discussed in the House. Through this Ordinance the 
Government has removed TRAI from the purview of C&AG. This is a very 
serious matter because C&AG has not taken a suo motu decision. The C&AG 
has thoroughly checked and investigated and has gone deeply into the 
functioning of the staff of TRAI. The C&AG has made a severe indictment 
of lavish expenditure by the members of TRAI during their trips abroad. It is 
very strange. Instead of controlling the lavish expenditure, the Government 
has unbridled them and has given them a free hand. These are the drawbacks. 
The Government will have to answer this question. Why have they done it? 
So far as modalities are concern ed, the Government has kept in mind only the 
views of the strongest lobby and the interested lobby. Where was the need for 
such a hurry? The Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Telecommunications was discussing this issue. Discussions were in progress. 
Meetings were going on and witnesses had been called to respond to the 
queries of the Members of the Committee. But the Government has 
completely bypassed and ignored the Standing Committee. Sir, this House 
cannot approve or accept this attitude of bypassing the Standing Committee. 
So, Sir, this House was not expecting any such ordinance. 
Ordinances are issued only when there is an utmost need or an emergency to 
meet some such issues which need immediate attention of the country and 
which are of very grave nat ure in larger interests of larger sections of the 
people. I do not want to use harsh words because of my respect for Shri 
Paswanji. But, as one of the great leaders, he has to explain why the 
Government had gone in for issuing an ordinance just for the benefit of some -
multinational companies. Sir, this House was expecting a full -fledged Bill on 
TRAI and not an ordinance. 
With these few words, I strongly oppose the ordinance and I urge 
upon the Minister that this ordinance be withdrawn, and that the right a nd 
supremacy of the House in discussing utmost, urgent matters in the House be 
restored and recognised. 
Thank you, Sir.
